interface.purpose: Write ~/.failproofai/jev.json (0600). --token puts the key in argv (warned). Mode off keeps the config but stops calling Jev.

interface.name: failproofai jev test | status [--json] | models | remove
interface.purpose: Live check of key, endpoint and answering model. Shows fallback reasons and latency. Lists models the endpoint serves. Removes the config.

interface.name: failproofai config [--status|--connect]
interface.purpose: Wizard: installs the root daemon, hooks every detected CLI, optional Cloud enrolment.

interface.name: failproofai policies [add|remove|show|--install --cli claude --scope user|project|local]
interface.purpose: Manage policy packs and hook installation. FailproofAI/jev-policies supplies the 16 Jev semantic checks plus 38 deterministic policies.

interface.name: failproofai (no args)
interface.purpose: Local dashboard on localhost:8020 with sessions, policy activity, and Jev settings.

interface.name: failproofai audit / flush / update / uninstall
interface.purpose: Offline audit of session history, telemetry flush, upgrade, hook removal.

interface.name: Hook events (Claude Code)
interface.purpose: Installs one failproofai entry per event for about 28 events (HOOK_EVENT_TYPES minus WorktreeCreate, types.ts:1065), including PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, PostToolUse, SessionStart, Notification. The Jev gate is only PreToolUse and PermissionRequest (handler.ts:248).

interface.name: Policy SDK: allow() / deny(msg) / instruct(msg)
interface.purpose: Custom policies dropped in .failproofai/policies/. Packs can declare authority hard|reviewable and semantic checks.

security: Key storage: ~/.failproofai/jev.json at 0600. A file readable or writable by others is refused, and hooks fall back to regex. ~/.failproofai must not be group or world writable, and setup strips those bits. The key is scrubbed from error text. Use --key-stdin. --token leaks the key into argv and shell history, and the docs warn about it.

Config is global-only. A repo-level .failproofai/jev.json is ignored, and the provider, URL and model are never read from env. That blocks a hostile client repo from redirecting Jev. Redirects are never followed (jev-client.ts:475). The URL must be https, or http://localhost in observe mode only.

Prompt-injection posture is deliberate. Hard policy denies are final, and Jev can never make a call more permissive than regex unless it read the whole call and was asked the exact concern. An oversized or cut call (request-cut) or a suspected injection withdraws all clearances but keeps Jev's own deny. A per-policy userCanOverride flag exists. The eval-noted weakness (injected text moving answers) is therefore bounded to clearances of reviewable policies.

Redaction before egress: redact.ts (2937 lines) redacts keys, bearer tokens, KEY= assignments, PEM blocks, URL creds and the process's own secret-named env values, and has an sk-or-v1 OpenRouter key pattern (redact.ts:820). Egress redaction is not a substitute for the no-secret-leak hook.

Third-party code exec: policy packs (JS .mjs bundles downloaded from GitHub) are loaded and run inside the hook process. FailproofAI/jev-policies has 0 stars, no license, pushed 2026-09-24. Pack digests are tracked (pack-manifest and pack-store), but its content was not audited here. The npm package pulls optional platform binaries @failproofai/failproofaid-<os>-<arch>, and the daemon downloader verifies SHA256SUMS.

Root footprint: the recommended `failproofai config` installs a system-scope systemd unit at /etc/systemd/system/failproofaid@<user>.service and runs sudo. The daemon does not see shell env, so the Jev key must live in the file. The hooks-only path (`policies --install`) avoids root.

Telemetry: opt-out PostHog (us.i.posthog.com, embedded write-only key). Hook events send tool_name, policy_name, decision, cli, event_type, and jev_* outcome fields (handler.ts:1042-1058). Install events send os, arch, os_release and hostname_hash. The npm install script hashes /etc/machine-id. Disable with FAILPROOFAI_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 or the config file. No prompts or commands are sent to PostHog (per the code read).

Compatibility with the user's setup: it registers its own entries on ~28 events in ~/.claude/settings.json alongside the existing hooks, and only touches entries it marked. `failproofai config` also hooks every other detected CLI.
Tests: 407 *.test.ts files, including dedicated hardening tests for the Jev client and redirect handling, envelope redaction and budget, combine and decide.
gh-failproofai-failproofai.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai, one POST per gated tool call (PreToolUse or PermissionRequest, when a policy with a semantic check applies), under the user's own key and with ZDR-only routing, data_collection deny and no fallback. The body has the tool name and input with secrets redacted, the recent human prompts (harness-injected text stripped), the agent's last message (labelled agent-written), and local facts (path relative to project root, git branch, permission mode). It is capped by MAX_REQUEST_CHARS, and an oversize call is cut and loses its clearances. Separately, opt-out PostHog telemetry carries event metadata (tool_name, policy, decision, jev_outcome, platform, hostname hash), not the payloads. Verdicts with per-question probabilities are logged locally to ~/.failproofai/state/semantic/verdicts.jsonl. Cloud tie-in (Failproof AI Observability) is opt-in via a machine key. With no token, nothing goes to Cloud. For client projects, the client's prompts and command text (redacted) do go to OpenRouter, so it needs a data-handling decision.
gh-failproofai-failproofai.failureMode: Jev failures fail open to the regex result for that call. Timeout defaults to 3000 ms (configurable 100-10000), and every failure is a recorded reason (timeout, http-429, out-of-credits, network, model-mismatch, malformed, and others). Client-side rate limit is 5 rps with burst 5. There is no circuit breaker, so a stalled provider costs up to 3 s per gated call until the user lowers timeoutMs (evaluator.ts:54-100 says so). The model must be Jev 1.13.x, otherwise model-mismatch falls back to regex. A hard-policy deny is never overridden. On a machine with the daemon configured, an unreachable daemon or a version skew fails CLOSED and denies tool calls. A broken pack denies the events its policies covered. Without a jev.json, or without a pack containing semantic checks, Jev is inert.
gh-failproofai-failproofai.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no skill. No token cost in context from tool definitions. Hook-injected text appears only when a policy denies or instructs (deny reason or instruct() message), and the Jev guidance for a warning is short. UserPromptSubmit and Stop hooks can add instruct text if policies are installed.
gh-failproofai-failproofai.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic. Every PreToolUse and PermissionRequest call goes through the hook, and Jev is consulted without any model prompting whenever jev.json and a semantic pack are present and a semantic policy applies to the tool class. Fires in bypassPermissions and auto sessions too, since PreToolUse fires regardless of mode. PermissionRequest only fires when a dialog would have appeared, so it is not reached in bypass.
gh-failproofai-failproofai.latencyImpact: Every one of about 28 Claude Code events spawns a hook process (node startup 100-300 ms per call on the non-daemon path), or a near-zero client to the daemon when `failproofai config` was run. On top of that, Jev-gated calls wait for the Jev answer: the code measured p50 about 500 ms, p95 about 1.7 s and p99 about 2.4 s on Cloudflare, with a 3 s cap. The Jev request runs in parallel with the regex policies. This stacks with gitnexus (seconds) and no-secret-leak on Bash, Read and Grep. Reads, Globs and other low-risk tools also pay the round trip unless the pack's tool-class applicability skips them.
pros: OpenRouter is native and correct: jev-client.ts:202 uses https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with typesafe/jev-1.13, Bearer auth, and provider {zdr:true,data_collection:"deny",allow_fallbacks:false}. `failproofai jev --url https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 --mode observe --key-stdin` is one command, and `jev test` gives a live check.

Very strong safety design for a model that is overconfident and injectable: hard regex denies are final, clearances require the exact concern to have been asked, oversize or suspected injection withdraws clearances, and any Jev failure returns the regex result. A pinned Jev 1.13 family is verified on every answer (model-mismatch), and observe mode records verdicts without changing decisions.
Config hardening is unusually good: global-only jev.json with 0600 and directory checks, no repo or env override of provider or URL, no redirects, key scrubbing, and a masked prompt or --key-stdin.

Covers the hook slots the user lacks (PermissionRequest, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, UserPromptSubmit) for regex policies, and 5k stars with daily commits, 1.0.9 released 2026-09-29, and 407 test files.
Redaction of secrets before egress is extensive (sk-or-v1 pattern included). A local verdicts.jsonl and a dashboard give an audit trail for tuning thresholds.
cons: Jev is not the product's core and is inert by default. It needs a separate external pack (FailproofAI/jev-policies, 0 stars, no license, created weeks ago) plus jev.json. It only sits at PreToolUse and PermissionRequest, so Stop, SubagentStop and PreCompact get only deterministic regex policies, not Jev. Jev use is limited to allow, warn, deny and clear-deny, not a Noul allow-fast-path like the OpenRouter cookbook hook (which grants permission). This tool mainly gates and does not reduce prompts.

Heavy footprint: a Next.js dashboard, a Rust daemon, and about 28 hook entries per Claude Code event in ~/.claude/settings.json. The recommended `failproofai config` needs sudo for a root systemd unit and hooks every detected CLI. The daemon fails closed on outages or version skew, which can deny every tool call. Doing the lighter `policies --install --cli claude --scope user` on the in-process path is the safer route.

Latency stacks on the existing hooks: a node process per event, up to a 3 s Jev wait on gated calls (p50 about 0.5 s), and no circuit breaker if OpenRouter stalls. The gitnexus hook (seconds) and no-secret-leak hook also run on Bash, Read and Grep.

Key handling gaps for this user: FAILPROOFAI_JEV_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY, is the env var, and the daemon ignores shell env, so the key sits in ~/.failproofai/jev.json in plaintext. It needs adding to the no-secret-leak protected list (path plus env var) and the file must remain 0600.

Data egress for client projects: prompts, tool commands and the agent's last message go to OpenRouter on nearly every gated call (ZDR-only, but a third party). It also has opt-out PostHog telemetry with tool_name and policy per call, so set FAILPROOFAI_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 or the config option. Commons Clause license, beta version (1.0.10-beta.0), and the pack executes downloaded JS inside the hook process.
gh-failproofai-failproofai.verdict: Best-engineered OpenRouter-native Jev integration found: safe fail-open-to-regex design, hardened key and config handling, and observe mode. It is a large, beta, root-daemon-and-telemetry-heavy product whose Jev layer only refines deny policies through an external new pack. Worth a trial in observe mode via the hooks-only install with telemetry off, but not a lightweight fit for the automatic-Jev-when-it-adds-value goal.

gh-doronp-jevc.name: doronp/jevc (jev-compiler)
gh-doronp-jevc.whatItDoes: TypeScript CLI/library (npm jev-compiler, bin jevc) that scans CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md style rule files, has the calling agent "lift" decidable rules into a Program JSON (narrow Jev Noul/Choice/Score questions plus a code reducer with thresholds), validates/lints it, and emits gates (SDK module, AI SDK, LangChain, JSON, bouncer/toolgate policy). The Claude Code plugin ships only one skill (/jevc:jevc, no hooks, no MCP). Optional step: the skill copies a sample gate.mjs into a project's .claude/gates/, npm-installs jev-compiler there and registers a per-project PreToolUse Bash hook. At runtime the gate builds state (tool_input plus last 4 user turns from transcript_path), calls Jev via @typesafe-ai/sdk POST /v1/systemone, runs the reducer, and emits allow (silent) / ask / deny.

security: Shell exec: no child_process/spawn in src (grep clean). Skill however tells the agent to run `npx -y -p jev-compiler@latest jevc` (unpinned latest third-party code execution) and `curl -fsSL <raw github pinned-commit>/gate.mjs`, and `npm install jev-compiler@0.1.0` into the user project; asks user first before touching the project.

API key handling: read from env only by the SDK (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as Bearer header; SKILL.md says never write key to files or print it; not in argv. redactErrorBody allowlist scrubs the API error body so echoed state is not leaked into messages (runtime.ts:~212-235, contract.ts).

Prompt-injection surface (a) rule files: jevc ingests CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md that may be attacker-influenced, listed as in-scope in SECURITY.md; the lift step is done by the calling Claude, and the skill relies on Claude to write program.json; citations are NOT verified by `jevc compile program.json` (SKILL.md section 4 says so and has the agent grep quotes manually). (b) Runtime: state sent to Jev contains tool_input and last 4 user turns; Jev is known to be movable by injected instructions in state, so a hostile command or file text quoted in a turn can push an allow verdict. Gate is advisory-quality, not a sandbox (SECURITY.md threat-model note).
Failure-safety of gate: sample gate.mjs exits 1 on import failure (missing jev-compiler), which Claude Code treats as non-blocking, so the gate silently turns off (SKILL.md step 1 states this).

Response-origin check: validateResponse refuses a response whose model is not jev-* unless JEVC_ALLOW_MODEL names it (contract.ts:65-81), protecting against a redirected base URL producing look-alike verdicts.
No telemetry found in src; only outbound is the Jev call. Apache-2.0, SECURITY.md with private reporting, solo maintainer with 7/30-day commitments.
gh-doronp-jevc.dataEgress: Per gated tool call the gate sends to Jev (api.typesafe.ai by default, or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points to, e.g. openrouter.ai/api) the state object: hook_event_name, tool_name, full tool_input (the whole Bash command, which can embed secrets or paths), cwd, up to the last 4 user turns of prose from the transcript, and project_rules text (gate.mjs:62-69), plus the compiled question instructions. Nothing else; no telemetry. Authorization header carries the API key. Observe-mode log (JEVC_MODE=observe) stores only answers, not state. With OpenRouter this data goes to OpenRouter and its provider; no local pre-redaction, so the existing no-secret-leak hook does not cover this egress, and it may not even see OPENROUTER_API_KEY in its protected list.
gh-doronp-jevc.failureMode: Sample gate fails closed: on any error (missing key, network, timeout, invalid response, non-Jev model) verdict becomes 'ask' (gate.mjs:29, 94-98; JEVC_ON_ERROR=allow flips to allow). Client timeout 5 s with 1 retry (runtime.ts:183-186) so worst case ~10 s hang per call. Caveats for this user: (1) in bypassPermissions/auto mode an 'ask' from a hook may still interrupt sessions, so an OpenRouter outage or missing key stalls every Bash call, or (with ON_ERROR=allow) silently disables the gate; (2) if node cannot import jev-compiler the hook exits 1 = non-blocking = gate off; (3) the ask/deny is a permissionDecision so it is a hard gate for deny. Unlike the OpenRouter cookbook there is no static prefilter, so every Bash call incurs a network round trip unless the user edits the matcher/tool filter.
gh-doronp-jevc.latencyImpact: Node cold start (~50-100 ms) plus network. README records min 695 ms, median 779 ms, max 2584 ms across 58 calls on api.typesafe.ai on one day (README ~L963-971); OpenRouter brief says p50 ~200 ms server side. gate.mjs exits immediately (no network) for non-Bash tools. Sample gate calls the API for EVERY Bash command (no cheap regex pre-filter), stacking with the existing gitnexus Bash hook that can take seconds and the no-secret-leak hook. Timeout 5 s x2 worst case.
gh-doronp-jevc.contextCost: No MCP server, no tools, no hooks registered by the plugin: zero tool-definition tokens. One skill; its listing description is 467 chars (~120 tokens) against a 2% listing budget; SKILL.md body 7,824 chars (~1,950 tokens) loads only when triggered. A deny/ask adds only a short permissionDecisionReason string to context. Generated gate adds no per-turn injected text.
gh-doronp-jevc.autoInvocation: Two layers. Setup: only when the user mentions enforcing/gating a rule, the agent ignoring CLAUDE.md, or jevc/Jev (skill description trigger), or via /jevc:jevc; it is authoring-time, not a per-task helper. Enforcement: once a gate is installed in a project's .claude/settings.json it fires automatically and deterministically on every PreToolUse Bash call with no user prompting, which does satisfy 'automatic use' but only for rules you compile, per project, and it must be installed project by project (or hand-moved to user settings with an absolute path and a node_modules-resolvable jev-compiler).
pros: Solves a real, specific problem: turns ignored prose rules (e.g. never commit unless asked) into reproducible, unit-testable deterministic gates; verdict is computed in code (runtime.ts runReducer), model only supplies evidence probabilities.

Genuinely careful engineering: strict validators for request, program and response, refusal of NaN/missing answers, redacted API errors, response-model check, fail-closed default (runtime.ts, contract.ts, gate.mjs).

Clean OpenRouter path for transport: SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY and hits /v1/systemone with Bearer, so env-only redirect to https://openrouter.ai/api works (sdk dist/index.mjs:56-62,513,554,581).
Strong offline test story: ~916 test cases, 58 recorded fixtures replay with no key, CI on Node 20/22/24; docs, SECURITY.md, CHANGELOG, Apache-2.0.
Zero context cost when idle: skill only, no MCP tools, no plugin hooks; gate output limited to a short reason. Observe mode (JEVC_MODE=observe) lets you dry-run a gate without blocking.
Can read transcript user turns so consent rules ('did the user actually ask to commit?') are answerable, which is exactly the class of rule static regex hooks cannot handle.
cons: Model id mismatch for OpenRouter: jevc hard-pins 'jev-1.13.0' and whitelists only jev-latest/jev-preview/jev-1.13.0 (contract.ts:17-25,134), while OpenRouter systemone uses 'jev-1.13'; needs a patch or a jev-latest test; unverified live.

Not automatic in the sense wanted: it is an authoring toolchain. Each rule needs scan, LLM lift, manual grep citation check, compile, and a per-project npm install plus hand-edited gate.mjs; reducer thresholds are guesses until measured (SKILL.md 'Finish').

Sample gate has no static prefilter, so every Bash call costs a network round trip (~0.2-0.8 s, up to ~10 s on failure) on top of gitnexus and no-secret-leak hooks; fail-closed 'ask' on outage interacts badly with defaultMode auto/bypassPermissions workflows.

Sends full Bash command plus last 4 user turns to OpenRouter unredacted; Jev is known to be steerable by injected state text, so the gate is defence-in-depth not a boundary (SECURITY.md says not a sandbox).

Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-18, 8 stars, 0 forks, no GitHub releases, 154 commits mostly in two weeks; corpus measured on one day against api.typesafe.ai only, never against OpenRouter; skill uses `npx -y ...@latest` unpinned.

Gate silently off (exit 1, non-blocking) if jev-compiler is not resolvable from the project; requires OPENROUTER_API_KEY to be exposed to hook process (and mapped to TYPESAFE_API_KEY), and it is not in the no-secret-leak protected list yet.
gh-doronp-jevc.verdict: Best-engineered candidate for turning CLAUDE.md prose rules into deterministic, tested Jev-backed PreToolUse gates, and its transport is switchable to OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL + key, but the hard-pinned jev-1.13.0 model id, per-project manual setup, no prefilter (latency on every Bash call) and fail-closed ask under bypass/auto modes make it a rule-by-rule power tool rather than an automatic daily helper. Use it selectively for one or two high-value rules (e.g. no unrequested commits) after patching the model id and testing live.

gh-greghavens-jev-no-bullshit.name: greghavens/jev-no-bullshit
gh-greghavens-jev-no-bullshit.whatItDoes: Stop hook (Python stdlib script, 1901 lines, plus an early-access Claude Code hook module hooks/jev.tsx) that reads the session transcript, splits the final assistant summary into sentences, and sends the summary, the user request, recent tool calls and results, and per-sentence and per-action Noul questions to Jev's /v1/systemone endpoint. The questions cover unverified claims (5 sub-questions), weasel words (2), empty rhetoric and paltering (per action). Scores above thresholds (0.65 for unverified, 0.7 for the rest) send the assistant back once per request with a quoted note. Supports Claude Code, Codex, pi and opencode. Every check is logged to ~/.jev-no-bullshit/log.jsonl.

providerSupport.evidence: jev-no-bullshit:38-39 DEFAULT_BASE_URL='https://api.typesafe.ai', SYSTEM_ONE_PATH='/v1/systemone'. jev_url() (1551-1557) reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL from os.environ only (https required, http only for localhost) and appends /v1/systemone. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api therefore yields https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which is the OpenRouter TypeSafe-schema endpoint. Request body at 1594 is {state, model, questions} and the response parser (1611-1620) reads answers[qid].noul, which matches System One. The key is sent as Bearer (1600). Blocker: the model is hardcoded, JEV_MODEL='jev-latest' (line 36), with no env override. OpenRouter expects 'jev-1.13', so 'jev-latest' may be rejected with HTTP 4xx. If it is, every check fails open with a warning on every turn. The README, tests and code never mention OpenRouter.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Easy but not zero-config. Two changes are needed. (1) Set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api in settings env. Any hook subprocess sees settings env, so the plugin works with this. (2) Change line 36 to JEV_MODEL = 'jev-1.13'. Either edit a copy (README 'Install without the plugin system': install -m 0755 the script to ~/.local/bin and add examples/claude-settings.json to settings with an absolute path), or use a tiny wrapper script that sed-patches and execs. The plugin install path is overwritten on update, so a manual copy or pinned fork is more robust. The OpenRouter key can go in ~/.config/jev-no-bullshit/env as TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<openrouter key> (0600). Reading the file wins over env, and the name only has to match TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
providerSupport.others: Codex (Stop hook), pi and opencode plugins. No other Jev providers.

interface.name: Stop command hook (hooks/hooks.json)
interface.purpose: python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/jev-no-bullshit", timeout 30 s. Reads the hook JSON on stdin (last_assistant_message, transcript_path, session_id, stop_hook_active) and prints {decision:block, reason:...} when flagged, or a systemMessage warning when unchecked.

interface.name: Hook module hooks/jev.tsx via hooks/claude-code.json (plugin.json 'hooks')
interface.purpose: Claude Code function-hook module (early access). Handlers: classic.Stop runs the script with JEV_NO_BULLSHIT_MODULE=1 and stores the feedback; turn.complete submits it as a new prompt via $.prompt.submit (instead of a Stop block); prompt.submit resets the redirect count and drops stale feedback. The plain Stop hook stands down when the module already marked the reply (module_mark_path plus reply digest).

interface.name: Environment knobs
interface.purpose: TYPESAFE_API_KEY (file ~/.config/jev-no-bullshit/env wins over env), TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_NO_BULLSHIT_MAX_REDIRECTS (default 1), JEV_NO_BULLSHIT_MAX_CALLOUTS (default 1), JEV_API_KEY (test harness only), CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1.

interface.name: tools/replay.py, decision_audit.py, collect_decision_scores.py
interface.purpose: Offline threshold-tuning and replay tools that use the harness key JEV_API_KEY. Not needed at runtime.

interface.name: pi/ and opencode/ TypeScript plugins
interface.purpose: Same check for other harnesses. Irrelevant to Claude Code.

interface.name: No MCP server, no skills, no slash commands
interface.purpose: Hook only. Nothing is added to the model context except the note injected after a flag.

security: Key handling: the key is read by the script from ~/.config/jev-no-bullshit/env (parsed, never sourced; a line with 'export' is refused). It is sent only as an Authorization Bearer header via urllib, so it is never in argv. Nothing is passed on the command line except the script path. The file is not permission-checked by the script; 0600 is only advised in the README.
https-only guard on TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (http allowed only for localhost/127.0.0.1/::1). Redirects are disabled (_NoRedirect, line 1540), so the bearer token is not forwarded on a 3xx.

Standard library only: no pip or npm dependencies, no shell exec, no subprocess, no os.system in the script. The TSX module calls $.process.run(['python3', script]) with an argv array, not a shell string.

No telemetry beyond the Jev call. No install scripts. The plugin is installed via claude plugin marketplace add from a 1-author, week-old repo, so pinning a commit or reading the script is the real supply-chain control.

Prompt-injection surface: the state sent to Jev contains attacker-controllable tool output (file contents, web pages, command output). An injected string could lower the flag scores, so the verifier can be evaded. That only fails to flag. An attacker cannot cause tool execution through this hook. A false positive makes the assistant re-summarise once, and the note is built from the model's own quoted sentences and truncated action labels.

No secret redaction anywhere in the script: no matches for redact or secret. Tool inputs (300 chars) and results (2,000 chars plus up to 1,000 chars of evidence lines plus up to 3,000 chars of outline) go to the API as-is. A secret in Bash output would be uploaded. The existing no-secret-leak hook helps by blocking many reads, but not everything.
Local logging: ~/.jev-no-bullshit/log.jsonl records the full summary and scores in plaintext (dir mode 0700). It grows without bound and there is no rotation. It may hold client-project text at rest.

Bypass-permission sessions: the hook is passive and adds no permission decisions, so it is compatible with them. It also runs when the model is unsupervised, which is where verification is most useful.
gh-greghavens-jev-no-bullshit.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or the TYPESAFE_BASE_URL host, i.e. OpenRouter then TypeSafe) on every Stop where a last_assistant_message exists: the full final summary (clipped to 30k chars and split into sentences), the user's task text, tool calls of the current turn (input clipped to about 300 chars, with up to about 300 chars of evidence from the middle), their results (about 2,000 chars each plus up to 1,000 chars of matched lines and up to 3,000 chars of line-start outline; clipping scales up to fit a 16k-token actions budget), up to 10 earlier actions in full and older ones as one-liners (up to 6k tokens), and the last 2 conversation messages (2,000 chars each) plus older ones as one-liners (up to 8k tokens). The total is capped near 32k state tokens. Content includes client code snippets, paths and command output, with no redaction. Locally, the script writes ~/.jev-no-bullshit/log.jsonl and state/*.json. On OpenRouter the request also passes through OpenRouter's infrastructure and its data policy.
gh-greghavens-jev-no-bullshit.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. main() catches all exceptions and returns an 'unchecked' systemMessage (line 1891). API/HTTP/timeout errors are logged and the turn ends normally. A missing key produces a warning, and the module pins it on the status line. Jev timeout is 10 s (JEV_TIMEOUT_SECONDS), enforced with a daemon thread and a deadline. The hook timeout is 30 s, and the transcript wait is up to 3 s. The auto-retry with a smaller budget on HTTP 400 max_tokens_exceeded shares the same 10 s deadline. Redirects are capped at 1 per request (JEV_NO_BULLSHIT_MAX_REDIRECTS), and each sentence is called out once. It cannot trap the model in a loop. Caveat: if the model name 'jev-latest' is rejected by OpenRouter, every turn shows an 'unchecked' warning (noisy but harmless). In Claude Code the module path needs the early-access plugin hook modules. Without them it falls back to a classic Stop block that shows a 'Stop hook error' row.
gh-greghavens-jev-no-bullshit.contextCost: Zero standing context: no MCP tools, no skills, no injected system text. Tokens are spent only when a summary is flagged: the note is about 100-300 tokens, and the assistant then produces a revised summary (Opus output tokens plus one more turn). Default cap is one send-back per request. Jev-side cost is about 5-15k input tokens per check for typical turns (about 32k worst case, 64k with questions), roughly $0.0002-$0.0015 per check at $0.042/M. Trivial pure-chat replies with no sentences or actions are skipped.
gh-greghavens-jev-no-bullshit.autoInvocation: Deterministic Stop hook: it fires after every assistant turn end with a non-empty last_assistant_message and needs no prompting. It does not fire on SubagentStop, so subagent summaries are not checked, but the parent's summary that relays them is. It runs in interactive sessions and bypassPermissions sessions alike.
gh-greghavens-jev-no-bullshit.latencyImpact: Every turn end pays: Python start, transcript read (up to 3 s wait for tool results to be flushed), and one Jev POST. On OpenRouter with p50 about 200 ms (but a large payload of up to 32k tokens and many questions) this is likely about 0.5-2 s typical. The worst case is about 10 s Jev deadline plus 3 s transcript wait, under the 30 s hook timeout. When a summary is flagged, the user waits for a whole extra Opus turn. The module path is asynchronous to the reply stream (the reply is shown first, then the check runs), which hides some of it. The 'unchecked' warning path on API failure adds up to 10 s.
pros: Fills the missing Stop-verifier gap with a deterministic hook: no 'use jev' prompting, and it works in auto and bypassPermissions sessions, where unsupervised false 'tests pass' claims are most costly (jev-no-bullshit:1740-1901, hooks/hooks.json).

Fail-open design that is actually implemented: the outer try/except (line 1891), a 10 s deadline in a daemon thread, no-redirect opener, and a cap of 1 send-back per request with per-sentence callout dedupe. It cannot loop or wedge a session.

Endpoint shape already matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api gives https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (lines 39, 1551-1557) with the {state, model, questions} body and Noul answers parsed as the System One schema.

Thoughtful engineering against Jev's limits: token estimation against the 32k/64k limits, retry on max_tokens_exceeded with a smaller budget, threshold tuning from replays of real checks (docs/statistical-decision.md), and a 'repeat callouts' limiter.
Key kept in a separate ~/.config file read directly by the script, so it is not in settings env or argv. Only https (localhost excepted), and redirects are refused.

Stdlib-only Python, so no dependency supply chain. Real test surface: about 118 test functions across 7 Python test files plus hooks/jev.test.tsx, and a CI matrix on Python 3.10 and 3.13 that also runs e2e tests against the pinned claude 2.1.281 CLI. The README states it was tested with Claude Code 2.1.281, close to the user's 2.1.285.
Very low money cost per check (about $0.001) and zero standing context cost (no MCP tools or skills).
cons: Model name hardcoded as 'jev-latest' (line 36), with no env override. OpenRouter documents 'jev-1.13', so out of the box against OpenRouter the check may return 4xx on every turn (fail-open, so a warning each turn). It needs a source patch or a maintained copy or fork. Plugin updates would overwrite the patch.

No OpenRouter mention anywhere in the repo, so OpenRouter behaviour (rate limits on /v1/systemone, alpha endpoint stability, 32k context, no SLA) is untested. The script's tuned thresholds are calibrated on api.typesafe.ai's 'jev-latest', which may differ from jev-1.13 (the eval brief notes calibration is imperfect).

Sends task text, code snippets and command output from every turn to a third party (TypeSafe via OpenRouter) with no redaction, and it is on by default for all projects. For client projects this is a real confidentiality and NDA concern. The user would need a per-project disable (project-scoped enabledPlugins or a path guard in a wrapper). Full summaries are also logged at rest in ~/.jev-no-bullshit/log.jsonl with no rotation.

The Claude Code send-back UX relies on the early-access hook-module API (hooks/jev.tsx, hooks/claude-code.json, $.prompt.submit). It is fragile across Claude Code versions (only 2.1.281 verified). The fallback is a 'Stop hook error' row using Stop block feedback.

False positives cost a full extra Opus turn (tokens plus wait time) and the verifier can be evaded by injected content in tool outputs. Evals show calibration is imperfect, so the utility is a probabilistic nudge, not a guarantee. It cannot check claims that are unverifiable from the transcript, such as work done in other sessions. Subagent (SubagentStop) work is not checked directly.

Immature: created 2026-09-23, 40 commits in about a week (33 by the author, 7 by Claude), 1 human contributor, 3 stars, 0 forks, no releases, and no license (licenseInfo null), so legally all rights are reserved and use or modification of the code is not formally permitted, which matters for client work. Version 0.4.0.

Latency of up to about 13 s worst case per turn end (3 s transcript wait plus 10 s API deadline), and the Jev call on a large payload may be slower than the p50 of 200 ms on OpenRouter's alpha endpoint.

The user's other hooks (gitnexus, caveman) are unaffected, but the OpenRouter key would sit in a second place. The existing no-secret-leak hook's protected list should also cover it, and reading ~/.config/jev-no-bullshit/env with Read may be blocked or need an allowance.
gh-greghavens-jev-no-bullshit.verdict: Best-fitting candidate for an automatic Stop-time honesty check: deterministic, fail-open, cheap, zero standing context, and its /v1/systemone request shape is OpenRouter-compatible via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. Before it is usable, the hardcoded model 'jev-latest' must be changed to 'jev-1.13' in a pinned copy or fork. The lack of a license, the unredacted egress of client code, and the week-old, early-access hook-module dependency mean it should be run from a pinned local copy and disabled for confidential client repos, not adopted as-is.

gh-coldteadotai-abide.name: coldteadotai/abide
gh-coldteadotai-abide.whatItDoes: CLI (@coldtea/abide, npm) whose `init` writes four Node hooks into ~/.claude/settings.json (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit|apply_patch, Stop). It compiles AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md into a committed .abide/rubric.json by asking the running agent to follow a bundled SKILL.md at SessionStart. After each edit and at turn end it sends the diff plus the rule questions to Jev (one Noul/Choice/Score question per rule). Rules scoring >=0.8 block with a repair request (PostToolUse feedback or Stop decision:block). 0.5-0.8 gives a user-visible note. Also has CLI audit/check/report/replay/calibrate/tune/bench for offline use. Supports Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode.

providerSupport.evidence: Jev is called only through the Vercel AI SDK provider @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai 3.0.3 (packages/cli/src/lib/jev.ts:163-169, createTypeSafeAi({apiKey, baseURL}) then provider.evaluationModel(TYPESAFE_MODEL_ID)). TYPESAFE_MODEL_ID is hard-coded "jev-latest" (constants.ts:2). Env vars: TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (Vercel gateway, model "typesafe-ai/jev", constants.ts:3-5) and TYPESAFE_AI_BASE_URL (constants.ts:8; credentials.ts:22,72-74,84-89). I read the SDK tarball source: default baseURL is https://api.typesafe.ai/v1 and it POSTs ${baseURL}/systemone with Bearer key and body {model, state, questions} (typesafe-ai-provider.ts:35-40, typesafe-ai-evaluation-model.ts:109-117). That is the same schema as OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone. There is no OpenRouter mention in the code or README (grep found only base-URL test fixtures).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Config-only attempt: put TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and TYPESAFE_AI_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 in ~/.abide/.env or the hook env. The URL becomes https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with a Bearer key, which matches. The blocker is the model id: hard-coded to "jev-latest", whereas the brief says OpenRouter's /systemone expects "jev-1.13", and there is no env override. If OpenRouter rejects "jev-latest", every check fails and is swallowed (fail-open), so it would look installed but never check anything. Fix is a one-line change to constants.ts:2 in a fork, or a local patch of the installed dist. Small patch, not zero-config. Unverified: OpenRouter response shape vs the SDK's typesafeEvaluationResponseSchema.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, zeroDataRetention:true). Self-hosted or mock via TYPESAFE_AI_BASE_URL.

interface.name: hook SessionStart (abide-hook.js session-start)
interface.purpose: Hashes instruction files, warns if no key, and if the rubric is stale injects additionalContext telling the agent to compile the rubric using .abide/compile-skill.md. Budget 8s (settings timeout 10).

interface.name: hook UserPromptSubmit (turn-start)
interface.purpose: Saves the prompt and snapshots the working tree with git as a baseline. Prints nothing. Budget 8s.

interface.name: hook PostToolUse matcher Edit|Write|MultiEdit|apply_patch (post-tool-use)
interface.purpose: Computes the edit diff, skips secret files and abide-owned paths, calls Jev once per edit for all edit-phase rules, blocks with a repair request at >=0.8 (max 2 blocks per rule per file per turn). Deadline 18s, edit timeout 8s (settings timeout 20).

interface.name: hook Stop (stop)
interface.purpose: Diffs the whole turn against the baseline, runs turn-phase rules plus edit rules for files shell commands wrote, emits decision:block with a repair reason. Max 2 Stop checks per turn. Deadline 28s, model timeout 15s (settings timeout 30).

interface.name: abide login
interface.purpose: Prompts for the key without echo and writes it to ~/.abide/.env or .env.local with mode 0600. Not via argv.

interface.name: abide init [claude|codex|opencode] [--project]
interface.purpose: Installs hooks and runs a self-test of the session-start hook.

interface.name: abide audit / check / report / replay / calibrate / tune / bench / compile / uninstall
interface.purpose: Offline audit of files, checking uncommitted changes, stats, replaying past sessions, calibrating or tuning rules, benchmarking, compiling the rubric, removing hooks. compile and tune spawn headless `claude -p` (claude.ts:16-31).

gh-coldteadotai-abide.runtime: Node >=22 (TypeScript compiled to dist; deps ai ^7, @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai 3, ink, zod, diff, picomatch). npm package @coldtea/abide v0.0.7. Hooks are `node "<pkgroot>/dist/abide-hook.js" <name>`.
gh-coldteadotai-abide.tests: About 25 vitest files (~119 it/test cases) covering credentials, hook, stop, settings, git, diff, band, sources and more. No .github directory, so no visible CI. No test hits a live OpenRouter. No GitHub release yet.
gh-coldteadotai-abide.install: `npx @coldtea/abide login` then `npx @coldtea/abide init claude`. Writes to ~/.claude/settings.json, or with --project to .claude/settings.json in the repo. Caveat: hookScriptPath() is derived from the package location (packageRoot.ts:8-28,32). Under npx that is the ephemeral _npx cache, so the hook command can break when the cache is pruned. A stable global npm install or a local build is safer. The hook command uses a bare `node`, which needs a PATH containing node (user's settings env overrides PATH).
gh-coldteadotai-abide.latencyImpact: Per edit the PostToolUse hook runs synchronously. README claims ~1s total, ~300 ms of it the Jev call, the rest Node startup with the ai SDK loaded via dynamic import (not measured by me). Worst case is the 8s edit-check timeout, 18s hook deadline and 20s settings timeout. Stop adds a git snapshot plus diff and one Jev call per turn, up to a 15s model timeout and 28s hook deadline. It stacks with the existing gitnexus and no-secret-leak hooks on edits, but only for Edit/Write matchers, not Bash/Grep. Jev's own 200 ms p50 to 600 ms p95 is not the bottleneck.
gh-coldteadotai-abide.contextCost: No MCP tools and no tool definitions. Hook-injected text only when the rubric is stale or missing: a compile prompt pointing to SKILL.md (13,286 chars, about 3.3k tokens, read on demand). Otherwise zero. Repair messages are a few lines each.
gh-coldteadotai-abide.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic: PostToolUse on edit tools plus Stop, with no need to prompt "use jev". It does not fire on Bash-only changes at edit time, but Stop catches shell-written files through the git diff. It only does anything when the repo or ~/.claude has instruction files with rules, and rubric compilation is done by the main agent at SessionStart (uses some of the user's model tokens once per instruction change).
gh-coldteadotai-abide.dataEgress: Per check, the Jev POST state is {task, file|files, diff}. `task` is the last user prompt from the transcript or saved prompt, truncated (MAX_TASK_CHARS 600, constants.ts:19; checkRunner.ts:100-104; postToolUse.ts:84). So the README claim that Jev sees only "rule + diff, never the conversation" is slightly inaccurate. The diff is bounded to 24,000 chars (MAX_STATE_CHARS). The questions carry the rule text derived from AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, so instruction content also goes out. Secret-named files and abide-owned paths are skipped (paths.ts isExcludedPath), but secrets hard-coded in ordinary source diffs would be sent. Destination is the base URL (api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if repointed, or the Vercel gateway). No abide-owned server and no telemetry found: the only network path is the AI SDK call in jev.ts. Local writes go to .abide/events.jsonl and ~/.abide session state (pruned after 7 days).
gh-coldteadotai-abide.failureMode: Fail-open by design. runHook (hookRunner.ts:20-55) sets exitCode 0, installs a hard-deadline timer that emits silent output and process.exit(0), and catches every error. A missing key logs a skip event and lets the edit pass (postToolUse.ts:73-82). Timeout, HTTP error or a wrong model id throws AbideError, which becomes an event and a silent pass (postToolUse.ts:101-111). The real risk is silent uselessness: with a wrong model id or base URL nothing ever checks and the user only learns via `abide report` or .abide/events.jsonl. Blocking is bounded (2 blocks per rule per file per turn, 2 Stop checks per turn), so no infinite loops. A false positive at >=0.8 forces a repair turn (extra Opus tokens). Jev is overconfident on ambiguous input, so expect some noise on subjective rules; `calibrate` exists to tame that.
security: Key handling is good: read from process env, then .env.local and .env at the repo root, then ~/.abide/.env (credentials.ts:76-92). Never accepted via a CLI flag or argv. `login` uses no-echo raw stdin (secret.ts) and writes with mode 0600 via O_EXCL and refuses symlinks (credentials.ts:132-150). The parser extracts only abide's 3 variable names from .env files. Reading is done inside the abide process, not via an agent tool call, so the no-secret-leak hook is not triggered.

abide does not read OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The OpenRouter key would have to be stored as TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, so the user's protected-vars list should cover that name too, or the key be kept only in ~/.abide/.env.

Installer rewrites the GLOBAL ~/.claude/settings.json in place (settings.ts:71-84). It keeps other hooks via a passthrough schema and removes only entries whose command contains "abide-hook.js". It throws on invalid settings rather than clobbering. It reformats the file as 2-space JSON. Back up before init. Use --project to limit it to one repo.

Shell exec is limited to fixed argv arrays: git (git.ts spawnSync), `node` for the self-test, and `claude -p` with --permission-mode acceptEdits and --allowedTools Bash(node *) Bash(abide *) for compile/tune (claude.ts). Bash(node *) is broad. No shell-string interpolation of untrusted data was seen.

Prompt-injection surface: AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md content is compiled into the rubric and appears in SessionStart additionalContext and repair reasons, so a cloned untrusted repo's .abide/rubric.json would be loaded automatically if the hook is global. Also, injected instructions in the diff can move Jev's answers and suppress a violation, though impact is low because Jev outputs only typed probabilities.

Hook script path depends on the npx cache (packageRoot.ts), so a cache purge breaks the hook silently (fail-open). `npx @coldtea/abide` runs a third-party dependency tree (ink, react, ai) from a 12-day-old org at v0.0.7.
No telemetry or third-party endpoints seen in the source (only the SDK POST). The Vercel path sets zeroDataRetention:true. TypeSafe retention terms are an account matter.
pros: Genuinely automatic and deterministic: PostToolUse on edit tools plus Stop with git-snapshot turn diff (hooks/postToolUse.ts, hooks/stop.ts), matching the goal of Jev being used without asking. Covers files written by shell commands via the Stop diff.

Safe failure modes by construction: every hook path exits 0, has a hard-deadline process.exit (hookRunner.ts:36-39), bounded block counts, secret-file exclusion, and a missing key or network failure lets the edit pass and logs it.

Uses TypeSafe /systemone through the AI SDK provider with a user-overridable baseURL (TYPESAFE_AI_BASE_URL); the request body matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone schema. OpenRouter is one constant plus one env var away.

Cheap and light: Jev at $0.042/M input, ~1-1.6k tokens per check, output free. No MCP tools; hook-injected context only on rubric compile. Rubric is a committed readable JSON with per-rule scope globs and banded thresholds (0.8 repair, 0.5-0.8 note).

Real engineering: ~25 test files (~119 cases), replay benchmark of 93 real sessions with published method, calibrate/tune/audit/report tooling, symlink and FIFO defences. Coexists with other hooks (removes only its own entries). MIT, no telemetry found, keys never on argv.
Project-level install (--project) writes only the repo's .claude/settings.json, which suits per-client isolation.
cons: Not OpenRouter-ready: model id hard-coded to "jev-latest" (constants.ts:2) with no env override, while OpenRouter's /systemone reportedly wants "jev-1.13". A wrong id fails silently (fail-open). Needs a fork or dist patch, and the OpenRouter key must be stored as TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY. Nothing in the repo tests OpenRouter.

Sends code to a third party on every edit: changed lines (up to 24k chars), rule text, and the last user prompt (up to 600 chars). README's 'never the conversation' is not exactly true. A concern on client projects. Secrets in ordinary source diffs are not scrubbed.

Synchronous per-edit cost: fresh Node process plus SDK import, ~1s per README, up to 8-20s on timeouts, Stop up to 28s. Stacks with gitnexus and secret-leak hooks on edit tools. Blocks trigger extra Opus repair turns and false positives on subjective rules cost real tokens.

Hook commands point into the npx cache unless installed globally (fragile). init rewrites the global settings.json. Rubric compile relies on the main agent following a SKILL.md, spending the user's tokens, and only works if instruction files exist.

Very young: created 2026-09-18, v0.0.7, 34 commits, essentially 2 authors, no GitHub release or CI directory, alpha OpenRouter endpoint with no SLA. Value depends on having many prose rules in AGENTS.md that linters cannot check; it covers rule compliance only, not general Jev use (no permission gating, no MCP tool).
gh-coldteadotai-abide.verdict: The best-built automatic Jev hook found so far: fail-open, tested, project-scopable, near-zero context cost, and it fires without being asked. Held to 6 because it is TypeSafe-only with a hard-coded "jev-latest" model id (a one-line fork patch is needed for OpenRouter's /systemone), it sends diffs plus the last prompt to a third party on every edit, it adds ~1s synchronous Node latency per edit, and it is a 12-day-old v0.0.7 that rewrites the global settings.json.

gh-alsoleg89-jev-guard.name: jev-bouncer (alsoleg89/jev-guard, repo renamed from jev-guard)
gh-alsoleg89-jev-guard.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (single-file stdlib Python bouncer.py, v0.5.0, MIT). PreToolUse hook judges Bash, Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit and mcp__* calls by sending a redacted state and typed Choice/Noul questions to the Jev /systemone API, then returns allow, deny or nothing. Hard-coded tripwire regexes can never be auto-allowed. A built-in read-only allowlist skips the API entirely. WebFetch and WebSearch get deterministic URL exfiltration tripwires only, with no API call. PostToolUse runs an injection sentinel on web, search, MCP and network-y Bash output and adds an additionalContext warning, or blocks with inject_action=block. It also writes a local audit log and cache under ~/.jev-bouncer and has report, calibrate and suggest commands. It also reads the Makefile target, npm script or script file a command names and judges that too. Defaults to mode=dry (log only, nothing enforced).

providerSupport.evidence: bouncer.py:46 URL = os.getenv('JEV_BOUNCER_URL', 'https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone'). bouncer.py:56 default model 'jev-1.13.0', overridable via JEV_BOUNCER_MODEL (bouncer.py:86). bouncer.py:488-491 api_key() reads only TYPESAFE_API_KEY or ~/.jev-bouncer/key, never OPENROUTER_API_KEY. bouncer.py:504-511 ask_jev POSTs {model,state,questions} with Authorization: Bearer <key> to URL. The body is TypeSafe's own schema, which is what OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts. Response handling reads raw['answers'][q]['noul'/'choice'/'probabilities'] and raw.get('usage',{}).get('input_tokens') (lines 642-643, 845, 965), which matches that schema. There is no OpenRouter-specific code and OpenRouter is never mentioned. A second backend, backend=openai (bouncer.py:572-603), targets any /chat/completions endpoint. It is a generic LLM-as-judge with a JSON prompt, not Jev, and is unmeasured.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Config only, no code edits. Set JEV_BOUNCER_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEV_BOUNCER_MODEL=jev-1.13, and put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY or ~/.jev-bouncer/key. That last part is a misnomer: the plugin reads no OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The env values must reach the hook process, e.g. via settings.json env. This is untested by the author and unverified here (no third-party code was run). The /api/alpha/decisions endpoint and the typesafe/jev-1.13 model id are not used. The full state can exceed OpenRouter's 32k context only if MAX_CHARS is raised; it is capped at 8000 chars (bouncer.py:50).
providerSupport.others: Any OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint via backend=openai (default Ollama localhost:11434); a local openjev-sglang server via JEV_BOUNCER_URL. Also Cursor and Gemini CLI adapters (bouncer.py:1404-1478, docs/adapters.md), described in CHANGELOG as never run inside those agents.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash|Write|Edit|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit|WebFetch|WebSearch|mcp__.*, timeout 15s)
interface.purpose: hooks/hooks.json runs hooks/run.cmd pre, a polyglot sh/cmd wrapper that execs python3|python|py bouncer.py. It emits permissionDecision allow or deny only when mode enforces it; otherwise nothing, and the normal permission flow continues. fail=ask emits ask on error.

interface.name: PostToolUse hook (matcher Bash|WebFetch|WebSearch|mcp__.*, timeout 15s)
interface.purpose: Logs Bash 'ran' rows. Scans results with the injection Noul question, but only if the result is at least 40 chars and Bash matches network-y commands. Emits additionalContext plus classifierContext, or blocks with inject_action=block.

interface.name: /jev-bouncer:report
interface.purpose: Runs bouncer.py report over the audit log and shows what would have been allowed, denied or deferred (allowed-tools Bash(python3:*)).

interface.name: /jev-bouncer:calibrate
interface.purpose: Replays the local log at other thresholds.

interface.name: /jev-bouncer:judge <cmd>
interface.purpose: Judges one shell command without running it.

interface.name: /jev-bouncer:suggest
interface.purpose: Proposes allow_patterns from deferred-then-run commands. --apply writes only user-named patterns into config or project_allow.

interface.name: /jev-bouncer:trust
interface.purpose: Marks the cwd project trusted so test runners and project scripts can auto-run there.

interface.name: bouncer.py CLI
interface.purpose: pre|post hook entrypoints, judge [--ask-jev|--edit|--mcp], scan (stdin), report, calibrate, suggest, trust, cursor and gemini adapters.

interface.name: Env/config
interface.purpose: JEV_BOUNCER_URL, _MODEL, _MODE (dry|guard|on), _FAIL (open|ask), _TIMEOUT (default 8s), _HOME, thresholds, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, ~/.jev-bouncer/key and config.json, per-repo .jev-bouncer.json (tighten-only unless trusted). No MCP server, no skills.

security: Key handling: the bearer goes in an HTTP header from urllib (bouncer.py:506-509), so no argv exposure. The key comes from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env or a plaintext ~/.jev-bouncer/key file (README suggests chmod 600). The plugin does not read OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

No shell exec of user data. The only subprocess/os.system matches in a grep for exec calls were none in the API path. Nothing is eval'd. The hook only reads files: it reads Makefile, package.json and script files up to 64 KB, refuses '..' paths and escaping symlinks, and sends a ~1500-char excerpt to the API.

Redaction: token-shaped values (ghp_, sk-, AKIA, JWT, Bearer, token=) are redacted before the API call, the log and stderr (bouncer.py:279). It is pattern-based and misses short or oddly encoded secrets, which SECURITY.md admits.

Prompt-injection surface: attacker-controlled command text, file excerpts and tool output go into the Jev 'state' as data. Jev is independently reported to be steerable by injected instructions in state, and SECURITY.md says identical input varies by about +/-0.03. Mitigations: tripwire regexes that can never be auto-allowed, hard-stop deny, allow only if p(danger)<0.10 and all risks<0.40. Untrusted repos' .jev-bouncer.json can only tighten (policy, policy_file, hold_patterns only).

Allow semantics: in mode=on an allow decision resolves in the permission layer and skips Claude's auto-mode classifier for that call. Per the README, Claude Code deny rules and explicit ask rules still win. mode=guard enforces deny only and never widens permissions.
No telemetry beyond the configured API URL. Local log ~/.jev-bouncer/log.jsonl (0600, redacted commands truncated to 500 chars, rotated at 20 MB) and cache dir (0700, 6 h TTL) hold command text.

SECURITY.md is honest that this is not a security boundary. Weak spots the author lists: shell state across calls, Bash curl/MCP exfiltration not covered by the web tier, and injection results only warned about after the model has seen them.

Supply chain: single-author, 1 star, 20 commits in about 1 day (2026-09-19 to 09-20), no external review. Installing it means running its Python on every hook event, so it needs a full read (81 KB bouncer.py), which was only partly done here.
gh-alsoleg89-jev-guard.dataEgress: Once a key is configured, even in the default dry mode, the following go to the configured URL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter after config) on every unlisted call: the Bash command (redacted, up to 8000 chars), the cwd absolute path, the agent's Bash description (300 chars), a plain-language policy from .jev-bouncer.md if present, and a referenced-script excerpt (~1500 chars from Makefile, package.json or script files). Edits send the file path and content or diff. MCP calls send the tool name and input JSON. PostToolUse scans send up to 8000 chars of tool output (head plus 2000-char tail) from WebFetch, WebSearch, MCP, and Bash after network commands. That includes the outputs of gitnexus and playwright MCP calls, which may contain client source code. Results are also cached locally. With no key, nothing leaves the machine. Web tools never trigger API calls. Client-project code and paths therefore go to TypeSafe or OpenRouter, and OpenRouter then forwards to TypeSafe. A per-project opt-out is not built in; it would need JEV_BOUNCER_MODE/scan/edits/mcp=off via env or config.
gh-alsoleg89-jev-guard.failureMode: Fail-open by default (bouncer.py:26, 1358-1363). No key, network error, HTTP error, timeout or malformed response makes the hook print nothing to stdout and the normal Claude permission flow applies. JEV_BOUNCER_FAIL=ask forces a prompt on error, in on/guard modes only. Per-call API timeout is 8 s (cfg timeout, no retry) inside a 15 s hook timeout, so a hung API adds up to 8 s per non-allowlisted call, and it stacks with gitnexus hooks. Missing Python means the hook is skipped (run.cmd exit 0). Missing key means judge is None for edits and MCP calls. Local tripwires plus allowlist still work without a key. Because fail is open, an outage silently removes the deny protection; it never wrongly allows.
gh-alsoleg89-jev-guard.contextCost: Zero tool definitions (no MCP server, no skills), and 5 slash commands whose descriptions are short (about 350-700 chars of frontmatter across 5 files, roughly 300 tokens if listed). No SessionStart or UserPromptSubmit injection. Hook-injected text appears only on a flagged injection (about 250 chars of additionalContext plus classifierContext) or a deny reason line. Effectively negligible.
gh-alsoleg89-jev-guard.latencyImpact: Author-measured p50 770 ms and p95 888 ms per API-judged call, on TypeSafe direct (README, docs/eval.md). OpenRouter's stated p50 is about 200 ms, which is not verified here. Zero latency for allowlisted read-only commands (about 51/77 routine commands), for tripwire hits, cache hits (6 h TTL) and web tools. Every other Bash, Edit/Write and mcp__* call pays one round trip on PreToolUse, and PostToolUse scans pay another for WebFetch, WebSearch, MCP and network-y Bash. Hooks run in parallel with other matching hooks, so the cost is not additive with gitnexus, but the slowest hook dominates. On a session with many gitnexus and playwright MCP calls, the PostToolUse scan of MCP output adds per-call latency and sends large outputs. It is meant to be silenced with JEV_BOUNCER_SCAN=off or scoped by editing the matcher.
gh-alsoleg89-jev-guard.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic: harness-run hooks on PreToolUse and PostToolUse, no model decision or prompting needed. It matches the requirement of never having to say 'use jev'. Defaults to mode=dry, so it does nothing user-visible until JEV_BOUNCER_MODE is set to guard or on.
pros: Real automatic integration: harness-level hooks on Bash, edits, MCP and web, no prompting; plugin manifest, marketplace.json, hooks.json and 5 commands all present and consistent (plugin.json, hooks/hooks.json).

Safe failure design: fail-open with optional fail=ask; hard tripwires that no model score can override (bouncer.py decide(), HARD_STOP); repo-local config can only tighten; mode=dry default and mode=guard (deny only, never widens permissions) fit a user running auto and bypassPermissions.

Directly comparable to the OpenRouter cookbook pattern but more thorough: local read-only allowlist skips the API (README: 51/77 routine commands with no call), 60-plus read-only shapes, reads what make/npm/script targets actually run, WebFetch/WebSearch exfil tripwires with no API call, redaction before egress and logging.

Switching to OpenRouter is configuration-only: JEV_BOUNCER_URL and JEV_BOUNCER_MODEL are honored (bouncer.py:46, 86) and the request body {model,state,questions} matches TypeSafe's /systemone schema that OpenRouter proxies. Only the key variable name is off (TYPESAFE_API_KEY).

Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no skill listing pressure, no injected text unless something is flagged. Stdlib-only Python with no deps, no installer scripts, no telemetry; key sent in a header, not argv.

Good audit tooling: log, report, calibrate, suggest, JEV thresholds tunable on own history; SECURITY.md is candid about limits; CI matrix on ubuntu and macos (Python 3.9, 3.12, 3.13); test_bouncer.py is about 80 KB of offline assertions with a fake HTTP server; eval.py with a published corpus and raw probabilities in docs/eval.json.
MIT license, latest tagged release v0.5.0, actively iterated (20 commits, single author).
cons: Very young and unproven: created 2026-09-19, 1 star, 0 forks, 20 commits by one author within about a day, no external users or review. The whole 81 KB bouncer.py would need a personal audit before trusting it to run on every tool call (only key paths were read here).

OpenRouter path untested by the author: default host and model are TypeSafe-only ('jev-1.13.0' vs OpenRouter 'jev-1.13'); it reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so the OpenRouter key has to be placed under a misleading name or in ~/.jev-bouncer/key. It does not use /api/alpha/decisions. No test covers the OpenRouter response envelope, and OpenRouter's alpha endpoint has no SLA, with fail-open meaning silent loss of protection.

Heavy data egress by default in scope: after configuring a key, even dry mode sends command text, cwd, edit contents and MCP inputs, plus up to 8000 chars of MCP/web/Bash output on PostToolUse, to a third party (then TypeSafe via OpenRouter). This is a client-confidentiality problem for the client projects unless scoped off, and there is no per-project kill switch besides env or config.

Latency: author measured p50 770 ms and p95 888 ms per unlisted call, and a PostToolUse scan on top for MCP, web and network Bash. It fires on every mcp__* call (gitnexus, playwright), each with an 8 s timeout budget and no retry. The 200 ms OpenRouter figure is unverified.

Fit for this user is partial. In bypassPermissions there are no prompts to save, so only deny/tripwire and injection warnings add value, and in auto mode a Jev allow skips Claude's classifier for that call. The allow path therefore weakens one safety layer for a model whose calibration is documented as imperfect and injectable. The recommendation is guard mode only, not on.

Eval is author-labelled on a small corpus (268 commands, 32 edits, 30 MCP calls, 34 results), the shipped thresholds were tuned on the same corpus, and OpenAI-compatible backend numbers are unmeasured. Results are non-deterministic (+/-0.03). The plugin says it is not a security boundary.

Overlaps and can conflict with the user's stack: existing no-secret-leak.cjs hook fails closed, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not on its protected list. The key would be visible in the environment of every hook process. It duplicates part of the OpenRouter cookbook's PermissionRequest pattern, which is lighter (a Bash-only hook that falls back to a prompt).
gh-alsoleg89-jev-guard.verdict: The best-built Jev integration for Claude Code: fully automatic hooks, tripwires that models cannot override, fail-open behavior, a local audit log, zero context cost, and OpenRouter reachable by setting JEV_BOUNCER_URL and JEV_BOUNCER_MODEL. Its costs are that it is 11 days old with 1 star, the OpenRouter path is untested, it sends command, edit and MCP output text off-machine, and each unlisted call adds a network round trip. Use it only after auditing bouncer.py, in mode=guard (never on) and with scan/edits/mcp scoped down for client projects.

security: Gate key handling is safe: the key is read from env and sent in an Authorization header via urllib. It is never put in argv or logged (jev_gate.py:164).
Static review found no shell exec, eval, telemetry or installer code in the repo. The gate and probe are stdlib-only urllib. The only subprocess use is the test file, which runs the local gate.

The gate sends the Bash command with a regex redaction pass (jev_gate.py:107-118: private keys, sk-/pk- keys, GitHub, AWS, Slack tokens, JWT, bearer, URL credentials, *_KEY/TOKEN/SECRET=value). It also sends the last user message from the transcript JSONL, up to 1500 chars, and the cwd. Redaction is best-effort. Secrets in file contents heredoc'd into a command, or in prose in the user message, can leak. For client projects this is a real data-egress concern.

Prompt-injection surface: the command string and user text go into Jev state, and an injected instruction could sway the answers. The design mitigates this because the gate never returns allow and has deterministic deny rules first. Jev can only make things stricter.

The gate provides no protection for OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the user's setup. no-secret-leak.cjs must add it to its protected list. The gate's SENSITIVE_PATH only skips its pass rules and does not block reads.
The installer chain (marketplace repo KHAEntertainment/marketplace, npx skills) was not audited. Installing by static copy avoids running it.
Deny rules are a best-effort regex floor and are trivially bypassable (base64, variable indirection). The README says they are not a sandbox.
gh-khaentertainment-jev-skill.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine while the skill is only installed. When the gate is wired in, each non-pattern-matched Bash call sends to openrouter.ai: the redacted command (up to 8000 chars), the tool name, cwd, the last user request (up to 1500 chars, redacted) and the fixed question schema, plus the OPENROUTER_API_KEY as a bearer. Calls short-circuited by the deny or pass regexes send nothing. The probe sends a static sample string. There is no telemetry to the author.
gh-khaentertainment-jev-skill.failureMode: The gate is fail-closed by design. Timeout, network error, missing key (KeyError on os.environ[key_env]), a bad response or bad stdin all emit ask, or deny with JEV_GATE_ON_ERROR=deny (jev_gate.py:184-201). The HTTP timeout is 4 s per socket operation, not a total deadline, against a 10 s hook timeout (the docstring admits this). A hook that hits its own timeout is discarded and the tool proceeds. For this user that is problematic. With defaultMode auto and bypassPermissions sessions, every OpenRouter outage, an unset key or a slow response causes an interactive ask prompt, and the skill states that ask prompts even in auto mode. In unattended bypass sessions deny mode would hard-block Bash. It is safe but can be disruptive. An allow-capable fail-open variant is not provided.
gh-khaentertainment-jev-skill.contextCost: The skill listing entry carries the full description of about 1.0KB (~250 tokens, from SKILL.md:3-15) and counts against skillListingBudgetFraction 0.02. There is no MCP and no hook-injected text. The SKILL.md body (~14.6KB, ~3.6k tokens) loads only when the skill fires, and the references (~52KB, ~13k tokens) load on demand. Idle cost is small. If invoked on a Jev task, the cost is a few k tokens.
gh-khaentertainment-jev-skill.autoInvocation: The skill auto-triggers only from its description, when the task involves building or debugging Jev, TypeSafe or a hook gate. It has no PreToolUse, UserPromptSubmit or other hook shipped in the plugin, so it will not make Claude Code use Jev automatically in daily coding. The only automatic Jev behavior is the optional Bash gate. That gate is a safety filter (deny or ask only, never allow) and does not reduce prompts in auto or bypass modes.
gh-khaentertainment-jev-skill.latencyImpact: Skill only: none. With the gate on: Python startup of about 30-60 ms per Bash call for the pattern-only paths. The Jev path adds about one OpenRouter round trip (p50 ~200 ms, p95 ~600 ms per the brief, plus TLS and cold DNS with no connection reuse, since each hook is a new process). Timeouts extend to 4 s or more. It is stacked in series with the existing gitnexus and no-secret-leak Bash hooks. It runs in parallel with other hooks of the same event, but a slow Jev call still lengthens each Bash call. Adds latency to every non-trivial Bash command (which is most of them) for no gain in permission-free modes.
pros: Accurate OpenRouter coverage from primary sources: both endpoints (/api/v1/systemone and /api/alpha/decisions), pinned and alias model ids, the docs-URL quirk, and per-path model-id mismatches that cause 404/403/422 (access-paths.md:13-17,90-154, SKILL.md:99-100). It matches the JEV BRIEF.

The gate is well designed as a safety hook. Deterministic deny and pass regexes run before any model call and there is a 3-question Jev call. It never returns allow, so it can only tighten. It self-enforces a deadline with a documented reason (a timed-out hook lets the tool proceed) and handles precedence. OpenRouter is a one-line env switch, JEV_GATE_PROVIDER=openrouter.
Stdlib-only Python with no install step and no third-party dependencies. Static review found no shell exec, no telemetry, and no key in argv. It has offline tests using JEV_GATE_MOCK.

Honest ops guidance: fail-closed for gates vs fail-open for optimizers, pin the version, calibrate thresholds, and a warning that thresholds are placeholders (TODO(calibrate)). It labels unverified claims. The skill has non-trigger evals so it should not fire on unrelated work.
MIT license, small footprint, and the idle context cost is only the description.
cons: It is a knowledge and template skill, not an integration. It does not make Claude Code use Jev automatically in daily coding, which is this user's core goal. It only fires when the user is already building a Jev integration, which contradicts 'never having to prompt use jev'.

The gate is a copy-in template with placeholder, uncalibrated thresholds. Its default provider is TypeSafe, so it needs env wiring, the key in the hook environment, an absolute path in the command (the snippet uses $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR and python3 from PATH, and PATH is overridden here), and adding OPENROUTER_API_KEY to no-secret-leak.cjs protection.

Poor fit for this user's modes. The gate can only deny or ask, never allow, so in auto and bypassPermissions it adds a round trip and extra prompts (fail-closed ask on any error) but removes none. It also sends command text and recent user messages to a third party on client projects, and the only mitigation is regex redaction. The OpenRouter cookbook's PermissionRequest fail-open-to-prompt pattern suits this user better.

Immature: 2 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, created 2026-09-23, no releases, no CI. It targets an /alpha endpoint with no SLA, and the Jev model itself has documented overconfidence and injection weaknesses. Dependencies on the marketplace repo (KHAEntertainment/marketplace) were not audited.

The 1KB description consumes skill-listing budget (fraction 0.02) for a rarely-needed skill. The gate's 4 s timeout applies per socket operation, not total, so the worst case can approach the 10 s hook limit.
gh-khaentertainment-jev-skill.verdict: A well-researched, honest, OpenRouter-correct reference skill, and a decent starting template for a Bash risk gate. But it only helps when the user is building Jev integrations, so it does not deliver automatic Jev use. Its one hook is a stricter-only, fail-closed filter that adds latency and prompts in this user's auto and bypass workflow, and it sends command text to a third party. Useful as a reference to pull ideas from (endpoint facts, fail-closed pattern), not to install as the answer.

gh-abhishekvrshny-jevexec.tests: 4 test files (core, jev, install, monitor), about 29 test/it cases, mocked fetch. I did not run them (static audit only).

src/updater.js auto-updates on every hook run, at most once per 24h: a detached background process runs git fetch and merge --ff-only from the author's main branch into the install dir, and that code then runs as your hook. It is opt-out via JEVEXEC_AUTO_UPDATE=0 and skipped if the checkout is dirty or off main. It is a live supply-chain channel with no npm install or signature check. Set JEVEXEC_AUTO_UPDATE=0.

Key handling is decent. It is sent via the Authorization header (not argv). The env file ~/.config/jevexec/env is 600 and rejected otherwise (env.js:306), with symlink refusal in install.sh:41. Prompt-injection surface: state includes tool command/path/url fields (safeInput allow-list, 4000 chars each), cwd and user guardrail text. Tool output and file contents are excluded. An attacker-controlled command string can still steer Jev toward 'low risk' and 'authorized'. The local HARD_DENY regexes are trivially bypassable (core.js:6-13) and the READ_ONLY allow-list is narrow. The redact() regex is heuristic.
Local audit.jsonl (600, capped 1 MB, keeps last 500 lines) stores redacted commands and paths, so secrets not matching the redaction patterns could persist locally.
No telemetry beyond the provider call and the git update check. No shell exec except spawnSync bash install.sh (hooks install) and git in the updater.
