max-automation.multipleMcpVerdict: ONE server, ONE tool. Register exactly one stdio server named jev (user scope, alwaysLoad true) exposing only jev_triage. Why not several: (1) The audited servers expose 1-12 overlapping verbs (ask, verify, screen, find, pick, extract, classify, rank, gate, evaluate). Opus chooses tools from descriptions, and the only measured adoption data are poor (0 of 150 unprompted calls for one bench, 0 of 18 sessions for a rank tool), so more tools add model confusion, not use. (2) Tool search is on by default (no ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL), which defers every MCP tool: only names and server instructions load at start, so a niche server's tool is effectively never discovered. alwaysLoad is the only way to make a Jev tool visible, and it costs context every turn: mine is 841 chars of instructions + 1,266 chars of tool JSON, about 585 tokens; four servers at roughly 2.5k tokens each would be about 10k tokens per turn for approximately zero extra adoption. alwaysLoad also makes startup wait up to 5 s for the server, so it must be a local node script (about 50 ms), not npx (your caveman-shrink already dies with CONNECTION_CLOSED). (3) Every extra server is another process, another supply-chain surface, and another egress channel that no-secret-leak (it does not inspect MCP arguments) and the brake cannot see. (4) Overlap: gitnexus already covers graph code search and impact, and Grep/Explore cover text search; the only thing Claude cannot do cheaply is bulk screening without loading items, which is one tool. LAYERING: hooks carry everything that must happen automatically (0 context tokens, independent of model discretion): brake on PreToolUse, webscreen on PostToolUse, stop-shadow on Stop. The MCP tool covers only model-driven batch judgment. The skill (about 80 tokens of listing budget, body on demand) fires only for application-code work and is worded not to match agent-side triage, so skill and MCP never compete. A 230-token CLAUDE.md block ties the three together (how to react to a brake denial, when to call triage, when to load the skill). Do not call Jev through mcp_tool hooks: their output is parsed as stdout, they are skipped at SessionStart/Setup, they depend on the server being connected, and command hooks importing the shared lib have none of those problems. What would change the verdict: if the log shows jev_triage called fewer than once a week by day 21, delete the server (the hooks do not need it); if you ever want a second Jev verb, add it to the SAME server.
max-automation.customGlue: WHAT EXISTS (written and tested in this run; no third-party code was executed, only my own scripts and read-only aggregate analysis of local transcripts): <scratch path> (tmpfs, copy to a durable place). jev/lib: jevlib.cjs 211 lines, shellclass.cjs 439, skeleton.cjs 68; jev/hooks: brake 104, webscreen 67, perm-gate 73, stop-shadow 50; jev/mcp/jev-mcp.cjs 99; jev/doctor.cjs and report.cjs; skill/jev-decisions/SKILL.md; install/{settings-snippet.json, policy.example.json, claude-md-block.txt, mcp-add.txt}; backtest/backtest.cjs; test/{classify,e2e}.test.cjs = 166 tests, all passing (132 classifier cases; 34 end-to-end against a LOCAL mock of the OpenRouter Decisions endpoint covering deny/pass paths, fail-open on timeout/500/garbage/out-of-range, key permissions, circuit breaker, kill switch, tamper rule, real temp git repo for the conditional rules, created-directory registry, skeleton privacy, MCP handshake, egress refusal, doctor). Node built-ins only, no npm install. Because only a mock was used, live behaviour of the real endpoint is UNVERIFIED (no key was touched): that the dated model id and provider.data_collection are accepted by /api/alpha/decisions is checked by doctor --live, with a printed fallback if not. INSTALL (about 30 min): 1) dedicated OpenRouter key with a $5 credit limit; in the OpenRouter privacy settings keep prompt logging off and restrict to ZDR endpoints if TypeSafe is listed; write it with umask 077 in your own terminal. 2) add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to PROTECTED_VARS in no-secret-leak.cjs and its test. 3) copy jev/ to ~/.claude/jev/, git init, read the code, run doctor --seal. 4) write ~/.config/jev/policy.json from policy.example.json and fix the roots. 5) merge settings-snippet.json (hooks, deny, allow), run the mcp add-json command, copy the skill, append the CLAUDE.md block. 6) node ~/.claude/jev/doctor.cjs --live. SHADOW PROTOCOL: brake_t1=shadow, brake_t2=shadow, webscreen=log, stop=shadow for 3-7 days. node ~/.claude/jev/report.cjs 7 --would groups would-denies by skeleton with the three scores; label at most 60 lines right/wrong. Day 7: brake_t1=enforce if unconditional-T1 false positives are at most 1/day (otherwise edit the tables: they are about 60 regexes, i.e. data); webscreen=warn if false positives are at most 2% on clean pages. Day 14: brake_t2=enforce only if at least 20 would-denies were labelled with precision at least 90% and none was something you wanted; if Jev adds no true positives beyond T1, delete the Jev stage of T2 (T1 stays and needs no Jev). Day 14: Stop verdict (graduate or delete; it expires anyway on 2026-10-21). Day 21: jev_triage adoption check. Optional 2-week compare_skeleton A/B; enable client roots in skeleton mode only if at least 95% of verdicts agree and the client contract allows command skeletons off-machine. REPRODUCE THE NUMBERS: node backtest/backtest.cjs 21 main|sub|all [skeletons] (about 25 s, prints aggregates and name-free skeletons only). MAINTENANCE: git + sha256 manifest is the only pin (no npx, no auto-update); when the logged response.model changes, re-run a 100-case probe set and the backtest; re-run the backtest quarterly; when Claude Code changes hook semantics re-run the 166 tests. NOT BUILT ON PURPOSE: any Jev allow path in bypass, Choice/Score primitives, ask decisions, output rewriting, function hooks, proxies.
max-automation.expectedValue: Measured, not assumed. Your recent traffic: 213 transcripts, 3,070 mode records all bypassPermissions plus 17 plan, 0 auto/default; last 21 days: 166,947 Bash calls (30,616 main, 136,331 in 5,794 subagent transcripts, median subagent 31 assistant turns, 93% Sonnet), 11,813 subagent WebFetch/WebSearch, about 6.5k unauthenticated subagent curl/wget/gh reads, 455 compactions, 14-16% of Bash under /Clienti/. WHERE JEV BEATS CLAUDE CODE BUILT-INS: (1) A command hook can get a semantic judgement in about 0.3 s with no Claude quota; the built-in alternative (prompt/agent hook, or a claude -p child) costs 1-3 s and rate-limit quota per call and cannot be applied to only the 2% gray subset. (2) Untrusted-text screening by a reader that is separate from the acting model, on about 870 unattended exposures a day where no classifier runs. (3) Bulk screening of hundreds of items without loading them or spending Sonnet subagents (cascade). (4) Knowledge for building Jev-backed features. WHERE IT DOES NOT: it is less accurate than Opus/Sonnet on code semantics (71.5% accuracy, ECE 0.19), overconfident (exactly 1.00 on 56% of answers), and steerable by crafted text, so it only vetoes or warns and never approves. In your modes there is nothing to approve: the flagship cookbook gate is dead code (0 firings), the auto classifier never runs, routing can only downgrade Opus 5.5, and on a flat subscription the dollars saved are about zero; the real currencies are safety, rate-limit quota (only via the triage cascade) and latency. BRAKE BACKTEST (21 days, offline): T0 97.5% main / 98.2% subagents, so the hook is invisible for the great majority; T2 gray = 2,894 commands (about 138/day, subagent median 35, p90 446, max 964) go to Jev; T1 = 317 (0.19%): 121 unconditional (about 6/day, bursty; force pushes including force-push to main, history rewrites, gh repo admin, outside-project rm -rf, plus agents writing to hook/settings files) and 196 conditional on live git state (mostly resolved as harmless on a clean tree). Expectation to be tested, not promised: T1 provides most of the protection; Jev's T2 stage will deny only a handful of commands a month (DELETE/UPDATE without WHERE, compose down -v, unlabeled deletions, gh api DELETE) but each is a potential data-loss event, and if shadow shows zero true positives the Jev stage is deleted at no loss. WEBSCREEN: expected to warn on rare mass injections in READMEs and pages; ceiling is non-adaptive attacks. TRIAGE: expected adoption unknown (public benches show discretionary tools are rarely called); kill rule at day 21. The single biggest lever your data shows is not Jev: 455 compactions in 21 days, addressable with a non-Jev SessionStart(compact) re-injection hook of pinned notes.
risks: Live endpoint behaviour is unverified: no key was used, only a local mock. Unknown until doctor --live: whether /api/alpha/decisions accepts the dated model id typesafe/jev-1.13-20260917 and provider {data_collection:'deny'} (the TypeSafe route may not qualify as no-retention, in which case requests 404 and every hook silently fails open; doctor prints the fix), response shape, and rate limits at bursts of 20-30 parallel subagents (429 -> fail-open + breaker).

Alpha endpoint, no SLA: a third party measured 50-63% 503s on 2026-09-28. Mitigations are built in (2.5-4 s deadlines, no retries, breaker, watchdog), but protection silently degrades to T1-only during outages; report.cjs shows fail-open reasons so you can see it.

Jev quality limits are exactly the ones the evidence lists: overconfident on unanswerable input, quantised/saturated probabilities, label-swap sensitivity (mirrored questions mitigate), injectable via command text or page text. Because the brake only denies and the tripwire only warns, an injected or wrong answer degrades to today's behaviour, but the tripwire will not stop an adaptive attacker (96.5% -> 26.5% under a crafted appended line).

False-positive friction: unattended subagents cannot ask you, so a T1 deny becomes a reported failure the lead must handle; the JEV_ACK=1 prefix is a cooperative override that a compromised agent could also type (this is accident prevention, not an adversarial boundary). Mitigations: shadow first, created-directory registry, scratchpad and repo-family roots, conditional git rules, labelled graduation.

Backtest limits: derived from transcripts, so project roots are approximated by the git top-level of the first cwd, created-directory logic is emulated, git-state rules are unresolvable historically, and today's research subagents inflate the tamper counts (about 45 hits in two transcripts). Numbers are for sizing, not precision claims.

Opaque commands stay invisible: make/npm run scripts, unresolved $VARs, code fetched at runtime and base64 content in gh api output cannot be judged, they abstain and pass. Jev sees only what the command text and evidence windows show.

Privacy: on personal roots redacted commands (<=1.8k chars), 400 chars of your last message, evidence windows, fetched public text and Bash read outputs go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. Regex redaction is best effort. Client roots send nothing by default; enabling skeleton mode needs the A/B evidence and a contract check. I could not verify OpenRouter's own retention setting for this account (check openrouter.ai/settings/privacy and the ZDR list).

Configuration risk: roots in policy.example.json are inferred from transcript folder names; a wrongly classified client root would leak. Default for anything unlisted is 'unknown' = no egress. Hook commands hard-code ~/.nvm/current/bin/node; if the nvm symlink changes, hooks exit 127 non-blocking (silent), so doctor must run after node upgrades.

Hook mechanics to keep an eye on: 'if' filters are best effort (the script re-validates); PostToolUse cannot undo a tool, only warn; a hook timeout is a silent pass; the Claude Code update cadence can change hook semantics (re-run tests after updates); 'ask' under bypass and function hooks are deliberately not used.

Environment: /tmp is a 31 GB tmpfs at 100% (26 GB in <scratch dir>, 4.7 GB jest_rs); a bash tool call already failed with ENOSPC during this run. Workflow scratch clones should be cleaned; the reference implementation lives on that tmpfs and can vanish.

Input hygiene: all inputs were treated as data; none contained actionable instructions for the agent. The existing secret guard blocked one of my own commands (a secret-file name plus a reader), which is evidence the *.key naming protects the OpenRouter key file.

Scope honesty: this is an evidence-bounded MAX-AUTOMATION design. It intentionally does not use Jev for routing, pruning, compaction, review, search, prompt steering or permission approval; another angle that adds those would add cost, egress and risk with no measured surface in your traffic.
max-automation.latencyBudget: Measured on this machine: node cold start 10.9 ms; brake T0 path 14.7 ms p50 / 17.1 ms p95; T1 deny path 15.2 ms; existing PreToolUse:Bash hooks run 18 ms p50 / 123 ms p95 / 2.8 s max (n=31,459) and run in parallel with the new one, so 97.5-98.2% of Bash calls see about +0-4 ms. Jev-bound paths (a hook process cannot reuse connections, so budget a cold TLS handshake): brake T2 about 0.3 s p50 / 0.8 s p95 (Jev itself 194 ms p50 / 633 ms p95 per OpenRouter), deadline 2.5 s; webscreen about 0.35 s p50 / 0.9 s p95 added to a fetch that already takes 1-5 s, deadline 4 s; jev_triage 2-4 s for 400 items (50 requests, concurrency 8, persistent connection), hard cap 45 s; stop-shadow 0 s (async); perm-gate (dormant) 4 s deadline. Expected added time: about 6 ms per Bash call on average, about 0.12 s per 20-call turn, about 30-45 s/day for the brake plus about 5 min/day for webscreen, aggregated across parallel agents (per agent negligible). Worst case during an outage: the first 5 failing calls each add 2.5 s (brake) or 4 s (web), then the breaker opens for 5 minutes and added latency is 0; watchdog exits at 5.2 s (brake) / 7.2 s (web) before Claude Code's own timeout, and a timed-out hook is a pass. Not on any turn path: bulk triage happens only when Claude calls the tool.
max-automation.costEstimate: Jev price $0.042 per 1M input tokens, output free (about $0.0000168 for a 400-token call per OpenRouter). Token sizes: brake T2 about 1.1k tokens = $0.00005; webscreen 0.5-3.4k tokens = $0.00003-0.00014 (avg $0.00008); triage 8 items per request about 1.7k tokens = $0.00007, 400 items about $0.004; stop-shadow about $0.00005. Measured-volume day (from 21-day averages, client roots excluded): brake about 120 calls = $0.006, webscreen about 880 exposures = $0.07, triage a few calls = $0.01-0.02, stop <= 10 calls = $0.0005, total about $0.10/day (about $3/month). Heavy day like 2026-09-29 (32.7k Bash calls, about 960 T2) roughly $0.3, covered by the $0.50/day hard cap (about $15/month worst case), and the OpenRouter key carries a $5 credit limit. On your stated nominal profile (300 tool calls, 40 prompts/day) it is about $0.002/day. Claude subscription quota: none consumed by any Jev call; the triage cascade is the only place quota can be saved.
max-automation.privacy: Default-deny egress by project root: policy.roots.personal = full, client = off, anything unlisted = unknown = off (about 84-86% of your Bash activity is outside /Clienti/, so client=off costs little coverage). Client roots still get the deterministic T1 brake locally; optional skeleton mode sends only program, subcommand, flags, path class (<in-project>, <home/.ssh>, </etc/...>), URL host class, SQL keywords with identifiers and literals masked and heredoc keyword lists, tested to carry no hostnames, table names or credentials; enable it only after the compare_skeleton A/B (>=95% agreement) and a contract check. What leaves the machine on personal roots: brake T2 = redacted command (<=1.5k+300 chars, project path abbreviated), up to 5 short code windows, git facts, 200 chars of agent description and 400 chars of your last message; webscreen = public web text (WebFetch/WebSearch everywhere, Bash network-read output on personal roots only, never authenticated calls, host only, no URL/query); triage = item texts (<=700 chars) on personal roots; stop-shadow = final message + tool log lines (personal only). Never sent: keys, tool output from client roots, files not passed explicitly, transcripts. Redaction: sk-or/sk-ant/sk-*, ghp_/github_pat_, AKIA, xox*, JWT, PEM blocks, Authorization/Bearer, URL userinfo, *_KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASSWORD=value, emails, 40+ char blobs; items with private-key headers are skipped. Data policy: requests ask provider.data_collection='deny'; OpenRouter's provider record for TypeSafe shows training false, retainsPrompts false, canPublish false and TypeSafe states it does not train on input, but direct TypeSafe ZDR is enterprise-only and OpenRouter has its own logging setting: check openrouter.ai/settings/privacy and the ZDR list, and use a dedicated key. Key handling compatible with your guard: file ~/.config/jev/openrouter.key (0600, *.key so no-secret-leak already blocks Claude's Bash/Read/Grep on it), deny rules on the config dirs, OPENROUTER_API_KEY added to PROTECTED_VARS, never in env, argv, ~/.claude.json or settings.json, endpoint host pinned so no repo file can redirect it. Local logs (0600, 30 days) hold redacted commands on personal roots and skeletons elsewhere. Supply chain: zero third-party runtime code (Node built-ins), no npx/npm/auto-update, pinned by git + sha256 manifest verified by doctor; the only external artifacts are the OpenRouter API and, in generated app code, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 by reference.
max-automation.isJevWorthIt: Yes, narrowly, and only in the shape your traffic supports; no as a general layer. Worth it: (1) the deny-only brake, because you run 100% bypassPermissions with 82% of Bash calls inside unattended Sonnet subagents and nothing else adjudicates, and a wrong Jev answer can only equal today's behaviour; (2) the injection tripwire, because about 870 untrusted text ingestions a day happen with no classifier and no human; (3) one bulk-triage tool, because that is the one thing Claude cannot do without spending quota or context; (4) the app-building skill, because it costs nothing. Not worth it: permission auto-approval (0 firings; the cookbook gate ships OFF), routing, pruning, compaction, review, search, prompt steering, Stop blocking, or any third-party Jev plugin (every bestPick has a verified defect and the ecosystem is under three weeks old). Total: about 1.2k lines of custom code you can read in an afternoon, about $3/month, about 15 ms on the common path, egress off for client roots. If forced to a minimum: T1 brake + webscreen + skill. Retirement rules are built in: delete the Jev stage of T2 if shadow shows no true positives beyond T1, delete stop-shadow after 2 weeks unless it graduates, delete the MCP server if triage is called less than once a week. Unproven until shadow data exists: T2 precision, webscreen false-positive rate, live endpoint behaviour (run doctor --live first).

scores.angle: PRAGMATIC-MINIMAL (one vendored skill + one PermissionRequest gate that starts as a prompt counter)
scores.strengths: Weighted 7.2 (value 4, automatic 4, reliability 9.5, latency 10, privacy 9, supply chain 9.5, maintenance 8, OpenRouter 7.5, Claude Code correctness 8.5). Correctly saw that PermissionRequest only runs when a prompt would show, so it is nearly dead in auto/bypass; my own count confirms it on your data (22 days of main transcripts: 2,762 bypassPermissions, 17 plan, 0 auto/default). Best knowledge component: the official typesafe-ai skill vendored at a pinned commit (sha256 re-verified today; that commit is still the newest upstream commit touching the file; 2,469 stars, MIT), description cut 679->469 chars because rarely used skills lose their description first when the 2% listing budget overflows (docs confirm), plus an OpenRouter/consent/call-site addendum. Key file named .env, which I verified your guard really protects. Zero hot-path cost, no third-party code, staged counter->shadow->allow-only gate with delete criteria. Its 28 tests pass (re-run).
scores.weaknesses: Delivers almost nothing on the Claude Code side for this user: its own delete rule (<10 prompts/week in default/acceptEdits/plan) fires immediately on the real data, leaving only the skill. Leaves the measured bypass surface unprotected: 137k of 168k Bash calls (81.6%) run inside unattended Sonnet subagents with no brake, and block-rm.sh is not wired. No injection screening. Never measured your traffic (it estimated the ask-path as 'nearly empty'). Uses the alpha Decisions route although the non-alpha /api/v1/systemone takes the same request schema. The closed-world allowlist gate is well built but solves a problem you do not have.

scores.angle: MAX-AUTOMATION, bounded by evidence (deny-only brake + warn-only tripwire + one triage MCP tool + skill)
scores.strengths: Weighted 7.4 (value 7.5, automatic 8.5, reliability 7, latency 8.5, privacy 6.0, supply chain 8.5, maintenance 5, OpenRouter 7, Claude Code correctness 8). The only design grounded in real traffic, and I reproduced its numbers independently: 167k Bash commands in 21 days, 81.6% in subagents, 98.1% T0 / 1.72% T2 / 0.18% T1, every session bypass. The only design with a mechanism that binds in bypass (PreToolUse deny; hooks-guide.md says it holds in bypassPermissions). Monotone-safe (deny-only, never allow), a deterministic T1 that needs no key, per-root egress policy with a skeleton mode for client roots, breaker/budget/watchdog, doctor/report/backtest tooling, warn-only web tripwire that avoids the unverified updatedToolOutput shape, `if` filters so curl/gh reads cost no process for other Bash calls. Its 166 tests pass (re-run).
scores.weaknesses: Config/state/git paths were overridable from the environment (JEV_HOME, JEV_STATE, JEV_GIT, os.homedir() honours HOME) and a repo's settings env block can set them. Key file openrouter.key is NOT protected by your guard (verified: Read, Grep and cat all allowed) although the design says it is. JEV_ACK=1 override is agent-typable and the deny text tells agents exactly how to use it. False-positive classes found by replaying your history: `git push origin main :old-branch` (protection judged on any ref in the command), scratch dirs under /run/user/<uid> and /dev/shm, a heredoc tamper heuristic that fires while building the hooks themselves. Enforces every T1 rule at once instead of per rule id, in the main thread too (14 of the 21 rule hits in 21 days are main-thread commands you probably asked for). About 1.2k lines to own; stop-shadow and perm-gate add code and egress without measured benefit; alwaysLoad costs ~585 tokens/turn; WebFetch/WebSearch is screened although it returns a small model's summary. T2 is a base-rate trap (few real dangers among ~2.9k gray commands) and rm -rf $VAR (23% of T2) is unjudgeable from text.

scores.angle: SAFETY AND PRIVACY FIRST (jev-cc: WebFetch tripwire + log-only permission gate + denied logger)
scores.strengths: Weighted 7.1 (value 4.5, automatic 5, reliability 8.5, latency 9.5, privacy 8.5, supply chain 9.5, maintenance 7, OpenRouter 8, Claude Code correctness 7.5). Best trust-boundary engineering: passwd home, argv-only test flag, env taint guard, 0600+uid checks, redirect:'error', ZDR forced (I confirmed today that 'TypeSafe | typesafe/jev-1.13-20260917' is on OpenRouter's public ZDR endpoint list), drift-to-shadow, twin questions, breaker, daily budget, a 24-case probe set. Uses the non-alpha /api/v1/systemone (OpenRouter's OpenAPI: same DecisionsRequest schema, example uses typesafe/jev-1.13). Async shadow mode means zero latency while measuring. Its 34 tests pass (re-run).
scores.weaknesses: Small surface, small value. The web tripwire covers only WebFetch, whose result is already a small model's summary (tools-reference.md), so the raw channels where an injection actually survives (curl, gh) are unscreened. The permission gate is log-only and dead in bypass; the denied logger only helps in auto mode; no answer to the measured bypass surface. Key file openrouter.key is not protected by your guard (verified), so its central privacy claim is wrong as written. The updatedToolOutput WebFetch shape was read from a binary string and never observed. It did not measure your traffic, so it is tuned for modes you do not use.

judge.winner: design-max-automation (MAX-AUTOMATION, bounded by evidence) as the base, rebuilt into a lean hybrid: measured-surface deny-only brake + official vendored skill + warn-only tripwire + one optional deferred triage tool, with the pragmatic design's vendoring/staging/kill-rule discipline and the safety design's trust boundary grafted on. Scores are within ~0.3 of each other (each has a different blind spot); max wins on the two criteria that match your goal (real value, truly automatic) and on being grounded in your transcripts. The synthesis is a patched, tested tree: <scratch path> (190 tests + 28 shelf tests pass, manifest sealed; copy it out of the 99%-full tmpfs first). On the same rubric I would score the synthesis about 8.0 (my own score; no live run was possible).

final.angle: LEAN HYBRID, evidence-bounded: (b) official vendored skill + pointer for Claude writing Jev-backed app code; (a) a deterministic-first deny-only Bash brake for the unattended bypass surface you actually have, where Jev only adjudicates the ~1.7% gray zone and starts shadow-only; a warn-only injection tripwire on raw web text; one optional deferred triage tool. No proxy, no community code, no ecosystem MCP. Every stage has a numeric graduation gate and a delete rule.

stack.component: Trust boundary, key handling and guard hardening (no Jev decision)
stack.role: Makes the OpenRouter key compatible with the fail-closed no-secret-leak guard, bounds the blast radius, and stops environment or repo text from redirecting key, config, endpoint or git. Prerequisite for everything else.
stack.mechanism: (1) Key file ~/.config/jev/.env (dir 0700, file 0600, one line OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...) typed by you in your own terminal and read only by the hook/MCP process; never in env, argv, settings.json, ~/.claude.json or a shell profile. (2) no-secret-leak.cjs: add 'OPENROUTER_API_KEY' to PROTECTED_VARS (install/guard-patch.diff, one hunk, patch(1)) plus 7 new guard test cases (install/guard-test-cases.py). (3) permissions.deny += Read/Edit/Write(~/.config/jev/**), Edit/Write(~/.claude/hooks/jev/**) via install/merge-settings.sh. (4) Code: config/key/state come only from os.userInfo().homedir; the sole override is the argv flag --jev-test (a project env block cannot add argv); no JEV_HOME/JEV_STATE/JEV_GIT env; fetch redirect:'error'; env taint guard (NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, NODE_PATH, NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY and then the proxy vars, NODE_OPTIONS with tls/openssl flags => send nothing); git runs with a scrubbed env, fsmonitor and hooks disabled, --no-optional-locks; policy.json must be 0600 and yours or it is ignored; provider zdr:true + data_collection:deny forced; root class uses realpath and combines env project dir with the hook's cwd conservatively (any client => client, all personal => personal). (5) OpenRouter side: dedicated key 'claude-code-jev' with a $5 credit limit, prompt logging off, optional guardrail (model allowlist, ZDR, daily budget).
stack.decisionSpec: No Jev decision. Invariants enforced in code and covered by tests: never emits allow; fails open to the status quo; endpoint host pinned to openrouter.ai over https; environment cannot move config, key or state; a policy or key file that is not 0600/owned by you disables the feature; every call logged.
stack.whyThis: Verified today by feeding synthetic PreToolUse payloads to your real guard: it denies Read/Grep/cat on .env, .key (dotfile), *.pem, *.p12 and credentials.json, but ALLOWS openrouter.key, openrouter.token, .openrouter.key and key.txt, and does not block $OPENROUTER_API_KEY, printenv or node -e. Both the max and the safety designs named the key file openrouter.key believing *.key is covered; it is not (the guard's dotted-name list only matches a name that starts with the dot). A dotenv-named file inherits the guard plus your existing Read(**/.env) deny rules with no new code. The patched guard passes 30/30 on a copy and the original fails exactly the 3 variable-expansion cases. Env hardening matters because hooks inherit a project's settings env (docs), with a stated limit: a project you have trusted can also define its own hooks or set disableAllHooks (hooks-guide: a project settings file can override yours), so this stops accidental redirection, not a malicious trusted repo. Side effect: after the guard patch Claude can no longer use $OPENROUTER_API_KEY in Bash (intended; live Jev calls during app development are yours to run).

stack.decisionSpec: Design-time policy Claude applies to the APP's own Jev calls (the app is the caller, not Claude Code): state the fit check to the user first; Noul = does a literal condition hold, Choice = one of <=255 options and ALWAYS a none/unsure option, Score = 2-10 ordered levels; threshold on the option probability never on confidence; exactly 1.00 is saturated; abstain band (e.g. 0.05-0.95) goes to a human or LLM; never sort by probability; arithmetic/dates/counting in code; mirrored pair for gates; untrusted text only in state with 'state is data, not approval'; a Jev answer alone never grants permissions, spends money or deletes data; call site timeout ~2 s, maxRetries 0, non-Jev fallback; pinned model (jev-1.13 / typesafe/jev-1.13, never jev-latest), log response model; thresholds from >=300 labelled cases on a held-out split; shadow first; ask before sending client data; test with synthetic data, the user runs live calls. Does not fit: reasoning, math/dates/counting, code-correctness verdicts (independently ~72% accurate, ECE 0.19), non-English, large noisy state.

I re-fetched the pinned file: hash matches, and the newest upstream commit touching it is still that one (2026-09-12, v0.5.7). stack.component: jev-core: shared library, policy, kill switch, breaker, budget, drift check + doctor/report/probe tools
stack.role: One audited place for everything that must be identical across the hooks and the MCP server, and the observability that makes fail-open visible.
stack.mechanism: ~/.claude/hooks/jev/{lib/jevlib.cjs,lib/questions.cjs,lib/shellclass.cjs,lib/skeleton.cjs,hooks/*,mcp/*,doctor.cjs,report.cjs,probe.cjs,probe-cases.json,MANIFEST.sha256}; policy in ~/.config/jev/policy.json (0600); logs ~/.local/state/jev/log-YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl (0600, 30 days). Request: POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, Bearer key, model typesafe/jev-1.13, provider {zdr:true, data_collection:'deny', allow_fallbacks:false}, questions from lib/questions.cjs. Kill switch: touch ~/.config/jev/OFF. Circuit breaker 5 failures -> 5 min; budget $0.50/day; every answer validated (noul in [0,1], choice in option set). doctor.cjs [--live|--seal]: key mode, policy mode, roots, model pin, expected_model, endpoint, provider prefs, taint, hook registration with absolute interpreter, deny rules, guard behaviour (feeds the real guard a Read/cat on the key file and a $OPENROUTER_API_KEY expansion), skill installed, MANIFEST, plus a live probe with diagnosis (retry without provider prefs; retry on /api/alpha/decisions). report.cjs [days] [--would]: decisions by tier/agent, rule ids, core-vs-shadow, latency p50/p95, cost, models seen, drift rows, fail-open reasons, error rate, last successful Jev call. probe.cjs [--save-baseline]: 12 synthetic web texts + 12 brake gray-zone commands through the same questions and thresholds; compares verdicts with the saved baseline.
stack.decisionSpec: Model pinned by family (typesafe/jev-1.13); after 'doctor --live' set policy.expected_model to the dated snapshot the response reports (OpenRouter's catalog shows canonical slug typesafe/jev-1.13-20260917). A response model different from expected_model = drift: T2 never enforces, rows are marked, report shows it, probe must be re-run and the baseline re-saved after re-labelling. Roots: personal/client/unknown; egress: personal full, client off, unknown off; public web text also for unknown roots (policy.web_root_classes), never for client.
stack.whyThis: Every audited community candidate failed one of: repo-controlled endpoint or consent, key in argv/settings, silent misconfiguration, no breaker, no kill switch. The chosen route is /api/v1/systemone rather than /alpha: OpenRouter's OpenAPI tags only alpha.decisions as alpha, both share DecisionsRequest (state may be a string, object or array; provider preferences include zdr, data_collection, allow_fallbacks with additionalProperties:false; noul criteria optional but need both true/false when present), and both routes answered 401 to an unauthenticated POST today while an unknown route answered 404. The catalog lists typesafe/jev-1.13 (32k context, $0.042/M in, $0 out, text->decisions) and the ZDR list contains the TypeSafe endpoint. Not verified: any authenticated call (no key was used) - doctor --live is the acceptance test.
stack.config: ~/.config/jev/policy.json from install/policy.example.json: {"mode":{"brake_t1":"shadow","brake_t2":"shadow","webscreen":"log","triage":"on"},"t1_enforce":"core","t1_scope":"subagents","t2_enforce":[],"roots":{"personal":["<personal root>","<personal root 2>"],"client":["<client root>","<client root>"]},"egress":{"personal":"full","client":"off","unknown":"off"},"web_root_classes":["personal","unknown"],"web_trusted_hosts":[],"budget_usd_day":0.5}  (then add "expected_model" from doctor --live). Classify <dev root>/* and <websites root>/* yourself: 72.5% of your Bash calls are in roots that are 'unknown' until you do.

stack.component: jev-brake: deny-only Bash brake (PreToolUse), deterministic T1 first, Jev only in the gray zone
stack.role: Claude Code's own decisions (meaning a): the only mechanism that binds in your bypassPermissions sessions, where 81.6% of Bash calls run inside unattended Sonnet subagents with no prompt and no classifier. Insurance against rare irreversible commands; T1 needs no key and no egress.
stack.mechanism: PreToolUse, matcher Bash, exec form: command ~/.nvm/current/bin/node, args [~/.claude/hooks/jev/hooks/brake.cjs], timeout 6 s, internal watchdog 5.2 s. Runs in parallel with no-secret-leak and gitnexus. Output is empty or one hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision='deny' object; never allow/ask (a hook ask in bypass is undocumented; deny is documented to hold in bypassPermissions). Human override: shell-mode '!' (docs: runs directly without going through Claude, so it does not pass through the Bash tool); there is no agent-typable override.
stack.decisionSpec: T0 (98.1% of replayed commands): silent pass. T1 deterministic (0.18%): ~40 rules from a quote-aware lexer (heredocs, $(), bash -c, referenced scripts). Default enforcement = 'core' set AND only inside subagents (hook input has agent_id): fork bomb, disk admin/dd to device, kill -1, crontab -r, git history rewrite/reflog expire/gc --prune=now, git clean -x, gh repo delete/archive/transfer, rm of root/home/.git, wide find -delete, git push --force/+ref/--mirror/delete or lease on a protected branch (main|master|prod*|release*|trunk|live|stable; protection judged on the refs being deleted, not on any ref in the command), direct writes to hook/policy/settings paths, terraform destroy, kubectl delete ns/node/pv/crd. Conditional git-discard rules (reset --hard, checkout -f, clean -f, restore ., checkout -- .) resolve with a scrubbed live git status and stay shadow until labelled; rm -rf outside the project stays shadow (scratch dirs /tmp, /dev/shm, /run/user/<uid>, ~/.cache and dirs the session created are exempt). Main-thread hits are logged as would_deny only (the human is the guard). T2 gray (1.72%): Jev, personal roots only, one request with three Noul questions: irreversible, contained (mirror), wanted (last real user message, main transcript); deny iff irreversible>=0.90 AND contained<=0.25 AND NOT wanted>=0.60; deadline 2.5 s, no retry; shadow-only by default (t2_enforce: []), enforced per rule id after graduation; drift => shadow; rm -rf "$VAR" (23% of T2) is logged as unjudgeable and never sent. Fail-open: timeout, non-2xx, malformed/out-of-range answer, missing/loose key, breaker, budget, taint, watchdog => exit 0 silently. T1 never depends on Jev.
stack.whyThis: Measured, not assumed: I replayed your last 21 days (167k Bash commands; reproduced the architect's numbers). Tiers: T0 98.1%, T2 1.72% (2,869), T1 0.18% (306; 110 unconditional, 196 conditional on dirty git state). The default enforcement (core + subagents) would have denied about 7 commands in 21 days (3 rm -rf .git, 2 git clean -fdx, 1 wide find -delete, tamper) and shadow-logged 14 main-thread commands (9 force pushes, 3 history rewrites, 3 gh repo admin) - i.e. insurance for a bad day, not a daily win, and mostly NOT Jev. Replay also exposed false-positive classes now fixed with tests (main :old-branch, /run/user scratch, heredoc tamper heuristic moved out of the core set). Jev's added value is limited to the gray zone: independent evals put it near Opus on bounded action gates (100/111 vs 102/111) and tool-call risk (55/60), but it is overconfident, saturates at 1.0 and moves under injected text, so it may only veto, never approve. Base-rate warning: ~429 judgeable gray commands per 21 days reach Jev under today's personal roots (2,022 if Dev/* and websites/* become personal) against a handful of real dangers; a 1% false-deny rate roughly halves precision. Hence shadow-only, per-id graduation, and a delete rule.
stack.config: settings.json entry (merged by install/merge-settings.sh): {"matcher":"Bash","hooks":[{"type":"command","command":"~/.nvm/current/bin/node","args":["~/.claude/hooks/jev/hooks/brake.cjs"],"timeout":6}]}  policy: brake_t1 shadow -> enforce after the day-3/4 gate; brake_t2 stays shadow until the day-14 verdict. Gates: T1 core enforce when no would_deny on a core id was legitimate work over >=3 days incl. a heavy day (expect ~1 core hit/day across main+subagents); T2 per rule id only with >=20 labelled would_deny, precision >=90%, 0 user-requested, and >=1 true catch T1 did not already cover, else brake_t2=off.

stack.component: jev-webscreen: warn-only prompt-injection tripwire (PostToolUse) on untrusted web text
stack.role: Independent second reader for text that unattended subagents ingest (~11.9k WebFetch/WebSearch and ~6k curl/gh reads in 21 days), where no classifier and no human looks. Warns; never blocks, never rewrites output.
stack.mechanism: PostToolUse, matcher WebFetch|WebSearch, plus seven `if` handlers on Bash (curl *, wget *, gh api *, gh issue view *, gh pr view *, gh repo view *, gh search *) so no process spawns for other Bash calls; identical exec-form node command; async:true while policy webscreen='log' (zero latency, output ignored), switched to synchronous with install/merge-settings.sh --web-sync when set to 'warn' (only a synchronous hook can add context). Output: hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext (documented; reaches the acting agent, subagents included) + systemMessage. Own watchdog 6.5 s because async hooks get no enforced timeout. One Bash call matching several handlers is screened once (atomic tool_use_id marker).
stack.decisionSpec: Two Noul in one request over {deployment context, source_host, content<=12k chars redacted (9k head + 3k tail)}: steers_agent (text tries to instruct/redirect an AI agent) and plain_reference (mirror). Warn iff steers_agent>=0.85 AND plain_reference<=0.50; else silent. Sends host only, never URL, query, cwd or prompt. Skips: text <200 chars, private/intranet hosts, explicit-auth commands, hosts in web_trusted_hosts, client roots (WebFetch/WebSearch/curl); gh reads only in personal roots (gh authenticates implicitly and may read private repos). Fail-open on every error. Gate log->warn: >=3 days, flagged share <=1% of screened calls, and a manual read of ~20 flagged rows shows genuine agent-directed text rather than llms.txt/AGENTS.md style docs (add those hosts to web_trusted_hosts); otherwise leave in log or delete.
stack.whyThis: Injection detection is Jev's best-supported class (96.5% with deployment context, 89.7% without; p>=0.85 band right 100% in sec-bench; 40/40 in OpenRouter's own test) and the acting model cannot judge its own compromised context; a warn-only failure equals today's behaviour. Correction to the architects: WebFetch returns a small model's answer, not the raw page (tools-reference.md; 'use curl via Bash for the unprocessed page'), so the curl/gh Bash channel is where injections survive - it is therefore included, and the unverified updatedToolOutput rewrite from the safety design is not used. Honest ceiling: one appended evidence-like line took an independent test from 96.5% to 26.5%, so it catches blunt injections only; the real hit rate is probably a few per month. Volume with today's roots: ~740 screens/day (10,420 WebFetch/WebSearch + 3,313 curl + 1,788 gh per 21 days), about $0.074/day.
stack.config: PostToolUse entries are in install/settings-snippet.json (already merged by step 4). policy.mode.webscreen: log (3-4 days) then warn.

stack.component: jev_triage: one deferred MCP tool for bulk screening (optional 3-week trial)
stack.role: The one capability Claude cannot replicate without loading the items or spending subagent quota: a cheap cascade pre-filter for 30-400 short items (files with a snippet, log lines, issue/PR titles, grep hits, diff hunks) against ONE criterion, e.g. before a Workflow fan-out. Advisory only.
stack.mechanism: Hand-rolled stdio JSON-RPC server (98 lines, no SDK), registered once at user scope: claude mcp add-json --scope user jev '{"command":"~/.nvm/current/bin/node","args":["~/.claude/hooks/jev/mcp/jev-mcp.cjs"],"timeout":60000}' (no env block; the process reads the guarded ~/.config/jev/.env itself). Deferred by tool search: names + the 841-char server instructions load at start (docs), the schema loads on demand; no alwaysLoad (would add ~585 tokens/turn and a startup wait of up to 5 s). Workflow subagents reach it via ToolSearch. CLAUDE.md bullet 4 tells the lead when to call it.
stack.decisionSpec: Items go in state, never in instructions; 8 items per request, 8 requests in parallel, 6 s per request, 45 s total, cost cap $0.05/call, secrets redacted, private-key items skipped. One Noul per item against the criterion. Buckets: clear_no <=0.05, clear_yes >=0.95, else uncertain (deliberately wide: 1.00 saturation). Order preserved, never sorted by probability; trailer reports judged/errors/skipped, model, cost and a random spot-check of dropped items; >20% failures => isError and 'screen manually'. Refuses unless the project root class has egress 'full' (personal). Kill rule: <1 call/week by day 21 => claude mcp remove jev --scope user.
stack.whyThis: Bulk relevance screening is where Jev's speed and price ($0.042/M input, ~0.2 s) beat anything built in (~$0.004 for 400 items) and where its known weaknesses matter least (cascade, read the middle yourself). Adoption is the risk: model-discretion tools were called 0 of 150 times unprompted in the only public bench, hence a trial with a hard kill rule and a CLAUDE.md nudge specific to Workflow fan-outs. Workflow scripts are plain JS with no Node/HTTP API, so an agent (with an MCP tool) is the only way a Jev call can appear in your dominant workflow.
